options.a: Evacuate and ventilate the area, ensure affected people get fresh air and medical help
options.b: Neutralise the gas with an alkaline cleaner, then continue cleaning with the door shut
options.c: Issue the cleaner a dust mask and finish the job quickly before reporting it to the supervisor
options.d: Flush the bowl repeatedly to dilute the mixture, then complete an accident report form

distractorExplanations.b: Adding another chemical risks a further reaction and a closed door concentrates the chlorine; people must be removed and the area ventilated first.
distractorExplanations.c: A particulate dust mask gives no protection against chlorine gas, and continuing the task delays first aid and evacuation.
distractorExplanations.d: Flushing keeps the cleaner in the gas cloud; recording the incident comes after removing people and ventilating, not instead of it.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Incompatible chemicals can release toxic gases; emergency response is evacuation, ventilation, medical care, and investigation of COSHH failures. COSHH controls should then be reviewed to prevent a repeat.

options.a: Continue welding and upgrade the RPE to an FFP1 mask until the next annual examination
options.b: Increase general ventilation by opening doors so the fume is diluted across the workshop
options.c: Take the LEV out of service until repaired, use alternative controls, and notify workers
options.d: Record the failed result and schedule repair at the next planned 14-month thorough examination

distractorExplanations.a: FFP1 is the lowest filter class and unsuitable for welding fume; a failed LEV test needs repair now, not deferral to the next examination.
distractorExplanations.b: Dilution ventilation is not an adequate substitute for capture at source for welding fume and spreads exposure to other workers.
distractorExplanations.d: Recording alone leaves welders exposed; a failed airflow test needs immediate action rather than waiting for the next statutory examination.

options.a: Struck-by from vehicles because the corner limits visibility
options.b: Manual handling from lifting wrapped pallets in the aisle
options.c: Fire from combustible packaging stored near racking
options.d: Slip and trip from poor housekeeping in a pedestrian route

distractorExplanations.a: The blind corner raises vehicle-pedestrian risk, but the wrap trailing on the floor itself is a slip/trip housekeeping hazard.
distractorExplanations.b: Manual handling relates to lifting loads; the hazard described is loose wrap lying on the floor where people walk.
distractorExplanations.c: Pallet wrap is combustible, but loose wrap trailing across a walkway is primarily a slip/trip hazard, not a fire-load issue.

options.a: Avoid work on the fragile surface or use collective fall prevention such as guarded walkways
options.b: Provide each worker with a full-body harness and inertia-reel lanyard as the first control measure
options.c: Brief workers to walk only along the roof's bolt lines so their weight rests on purlins
options.d: Install a safety net beneath the roof after the work is complete to protect future visits

distractorExplanations.b: Personal fall arrest sits below avoidance and collective protection in the work at height hierarchy, so it is not the first step.
distractorExplanations.c: Walking on bolt lines is an unreliable administrative measure; fragile sheets still fail, so the hierarchy requires avoidance or collective protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Nets are collective fall arrest but must be in place before work starts; fitting them afterwards gives no protection for this task.

options.a: Forced ventilation for ten minutes, then entry without gas testing if no odour is detected
options.b: Risk assessment, gas testing, permit-to-work, standby person, and rescue plan
options.c: A permit-to-work and a harness, with the standby person entering to assist if needed
options.d: Gas testing at the hatch only, then entry by a single worker wearing a dust mask

distractorExplanations.a: Ventilation does not prove the atmosphere is safe; solvent vapour and oxygen deficiency must be measured with a calibrated detector before entry.
distractorExplanations.c: Standby persons must not enter to rescue; untrained would-be rescuers are a common cause of multiple confined space fatalities.
distractorExplanations.d: Testing only at the hatch misses stratified vapour, and a dust mask gives no protection against solvent vapour or oxygen deficiency.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Confined spaces need atmospheric testing, isolation, permits, communication, and rescue arrangements before entry. Ventilation of the tank is part of the same confined space safe system of work.

options.a: Issue a mobile phone and rely on the guard to call the control room if anything goes wrong
options.b: Pair the guard with a second guard on weekend nights when crime statistics peak
options.c: Assess lone working risks, provide reliable communication, and periodic welfare checks
options.d: Install CCTV at the gatehouse so incidents can be reviewed the following morning

distractorExplanations.a: A phone without scheduled check-ins fails if the guard is incapacitated; lone working needs proactive contact and escalation.
distractorExplanations.b: Covering peak crime nights ignores injuries and health emergencies on other nights; risk must be assessed for every lone shift.
distractorExplanations.d: CCTV reviewed the next day gives evidence after the fact but no timely help to an injured or attacked lone worker.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Lone workers face delayed assistance if injured; risk assessment covers violence, health emergencies, and communication. Emergency procedures for summoning help also form part of the lone working arrangements.

options.a: Toilets and drinking water, with washing facilities provided once the site exceeds 50 workers
options.b: Toilets and washing facilities at the site office, with drinking water brought by each worker
options.c: Drinking water and a rest area, with toilets shared with the nearest public facility
options.d: Toilets, washing with hot/cold water, drinking water, and changing/drying areas where needed

distractorExplanations.a: Washing facilities with hot and cold water are needed alongside toilets from the start, not after an arbitrary headcount threshold.
distractorExplanations.b: The employer must provide wholesome drinking water; relying on workers to bring their own is inadequate welfare provision.
distractorExplanations.c: Relying on public toilets off site is not adequate provision; toilets must be available on or near the site for the workforce.

options.a: Biological agents risk assessment with containment level, training, and emergency procedures
options.b: General COSHH assessment of disinfectants used, with gloves and lab coats as the main control
options.c: Fire risk assessment with a laboratory evacuation plan and spill kits at each bench
options.d: Health surveillance of laboratory staff with annual chest X-rays as the primary control

distractorExplanations.b: Assessing the disinfectants ignores the pathogen itself; unknown respiratory agents need a biological agents assessment with containment, not PPE-led control.
distractorExplanations.c: Fire planning and spill kits matter in labs but do not address inhalation of respiratory pathogens, which needs containment and biosafety controls.
distractorExplanations.d: Health surveillance detects effects after exposure; it supports but cannot replace containment as the primary control for pathogens.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Biological hazards require assessment of exposure routes, containment, hygiene, and health surveillance per biosafety principles. Vaccination is offered where an effective vaccine exists for the agent.

options.a: Barrier cream before work and nitrile gloves only when visible splashing is expected
options.b: Gloves compatible with the substance, hygiene facilities, and health surveillance if needed
options.c: Respiratory protective equipment and LEV, since H317 indicates an inhalation sensitiser
options.d: Annual hearing tests and lung function checks for every worker who uses or handles the substance

distractorExplanations.a: Barrier creams are not reliable protection against sensitisers, and gloves are needed for any skin contact, not just visible splashes.
distractorExplanations.c: H317 is the skin sensitiser statement; respiratory sensitisation is H334, so RPE and LEV target the wrong exposure route.
distractorExplanations.d: Health surveillance must match the effect; for H317 that means skin checks for dermatitis, not audiometry or lung function tests.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Sensitisers need skin protection, hygiene, possible substitution, and surveillance for occupational dermatitis. A substitution review should also look for a non-sensitising alternative.

options.a: Warning signs at the entrance when wet, with the floor mopped at the end of each day
options.b: Non-slip footwear for all staff, with the lobby floor polished to keep it clean
options.c: Entrance matting, warning signs when wet, and slip-resistant flooring where feasible
options.d: Retraining the injured worker on safe walking and recording it as a behavioural issue

distractorExplanations.a: Signs warn but do not prevent slips, and end-of-day mopping leaves the floor wet during the rain when people are walking on it.
distractorExplanations.b: Polishing smooth tile lowers slip resistance, and footwear cannot be controlled for visitors; matting and flooring tackle the source.
distractorExplanations.d: Blaming individual behaviour ignores the foreseeable wet-floor hazard; controls should stop water reaching the floor in the first place.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Weather-related wet floors need prevention (mats, drainage), maintenance, and temporary signage — not blame alone. Regular mopping during wet weather keeps these controls effective.

options.a: Maintaining communication, preventing unauthorised entry, and initiating emergency procedures
options.b: Entering promptly to rescue a collapsed entrant, provided the standby carries a personal gas monitor
options.c: Carrying out the gas test and signing the permit as issuer before the entrants go in
options.d: Assisting the entrants inside the space so the task is completed in less time

distractorExplanations.b: A gas monitor does not protect the rescuer; standby persons must not enter without breathing apparatus and a planned rescue.
distractorExplanations.c: Gas testing and issuing the permit are tasks for the permit issuer or competent tester, not the standby person's monitoring role.
distractorExplanations.d: Working inside turns the standby into an entrant; the role is to stay outside, monitor the entry and raise the alarm.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Standby monitors the entry, keeps log, and coordinates rescue — often must not enter without proper rescue team and equipment. The standby must not enter the space unless it is safe and they are part of the planned rescue team.

options.a: Noise levels from the compressor, workstation ergonomics, and lighting in the booth
options.b: Ventilation capture velocity, respiratory and skin protection, and fire risk
options.c: Paint storage quantities, waste disposal routes, and labelling of decanted tins
options.d: Workers' training records and PPE issue logs, with exposure checked if complaints arise

distractorExplanations.a: Noise, ergonomics and lighting matter, but a COSHH assessment focuses on the substance: inhalation and skin exposure to paint mist.
distractorExplanations.c: Storage and labelling are part of chemical management but do not verify whether the booth controls exposure during spraying.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for complaints is reactive; COSHH requires checking that ventilation actually captures the mist, especially for isocyanate paints.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Spraying creates inhalation and dermatitis risks plus flammable atmospheres — LEV and RPE are typical controls. Compliance with each paint's SDS also needs checking.

options.a: Banking the day's takings at midnight on the way home to avoid holding cash overnight
options.b: CCTV covering the till, with footage reviewed by managers only after an incident occurs
options.c: Two-person closing where possible, panic alarm, safe visibility, training, and police liaison
options.d: A written lone worker policy signed by staff, with a phone check-in at the start of each shift

distractorExplanations.a: A lone late-night walk to the bank with takings raises robbery risk; cash should be minimised in store and banked under secure arrangements.
distractorExplanations.b: CCTV may deter, but reviewing footage after an incident gives no protection or prompt help to the lone worker at closing time.
distractorExplanations.d: A start-of-shift check-in gives no cover at closing time, when robbery risk peaks; contact should continue through the shift.

options.a: Training on manual handling of linen bags, with gloves issued on request
options.b: Hot-wash laundry procedures, with soiled linen sorted by hand to save time
options.c: Hepatitis B vaccination as the main control, so other PPE can be relaxed
options.d: Training on infection routes, PPE, hygiene, and spill procedures

distractorExplanations.a: Manual handling is relevant but does not address infection routes, and gloves for soiled linen should be standard issue, not on request.
distractorExplanations.b: Hand sorting of soiled linen increases contact and sharps risk; sealed soluble bags and minimal handling are used instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Vaccination supplements but does not replace PPE and hygiene, and it protects against just one of several pathogens in soiled linen.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Healthcare and laundry biological risks need hygiene discipline and PPE against contact and aerosol routes. Vaccination such as hepatitis B is offered where recommended.

options.a: Reduced capture efficiency allowing dust to escape into the worker's breathing zone
options.b: Higher air velocity at the hood face, so more dust is captured from a wider zone around the wheel
options.c: Reduced fan load and filter wear, with no change to the operator's dust exposure
options.d: Increased noise from the extraction fan as it works harder to draw dust

distractorExplanations.b: Capture velocity falls sharply with distance from the hood; moving it away reduces, not increases, the effective capture zone.
distractorExplanations.c: Hood distance directly affects how much dust reaches the breathing zone; it is not a neutral equipment-wear issue.
distractorExplanations.d: Hood position mainly affects capture efficiency; the fan does not compensate, so dust exposure rises rather than fan noise.

options.a: Anti-slip paint on treads, with materials stored on landings for easy access
options.b: Clear treads, handrails, adequate lighting, cable management, and housekeeping inspections
options.c: Hi-vis clothing and safety boots for anyone using the stairway during work hours
options.d: Signs reminding workers to take care, with temporary lighting added for night shifts

distractorExplanations.a: Storing materials on landings obstructs the stairway and creates trip and escape hazards, even if treads have anti-slip paint.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE does not remove trip hazards on stairs; housekeeping, lighting and handrails control the hazard at source.
distractorExplanations.d: Signs are a weak administrative control, and lighting for night shifts ignores daytime clutter and missing handrails.

options.a: Operator training, outriggers on soft ground, and harness clipped to nearby structure
options.b: A lifting plan, ground check, and use of the platform as a crane to raise materials
options.c: Operator training, harness/lanyard where required, and exclusion zone below
options.d: Operator training, and use on slopes up to the limit the operator judges stable

distractorExplanations.a: In a boom MEWP the lanyard clips to the basket anchor point, not adjacent structure, which could pull the worker out if the platform moves.
distractorExplanations.b: Using a MEWP as a crane exceeds its intended use and rated load; it is designed to lift people with their tools and light materials.
distractorExplanations.d: Slope and ground limits are set by the manufacturer and the site survey, not by the operator's judgement on the day.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: MEWP use needs competent operators, suitable ground, fall prevention where specified, and overhead/underside hazard checks. A ground conditions survey confirms the MEWP can be set up on stable ground.

options.a: Entry when the rotten-egg smell is faint, with a dust mask and a standby at the top
options.b: Forced ventilation for 30 minutes so gas testing can be omitted for short entries
options.c: Gas testing at the start of the shift, then entry without monitors for the rest of the day
options.d: Gas detection, ventilation, trained entry procedures, PPE/RPE, and emergency rescue

distractorExplanations.a: H2S deadens the sense of smell at high concentrations, so a faint odour is no reassurance, and dust masks give no gas protection.
distractorExplanations.b: Ventilation reduces but does not prove the absence of H2S; continuous gas monitoring is needed throughout the entry.
distractorExplanations.c: H2S levels in sewers fluctuate as flows change; atmospheres need continuous personal monitoring, not a single morning test.

options.a: Exposure must be reduced below the WEL using the hierarchy of control
options.b: Exposure may continue if workers wear RPE while the breach is investigated
options.c: The breach only matters if the 15-minute STEL is exceeded, not the 8-hour TWA
options.d: The employer must notify the regulator within 10 days and record the exposure

distractorExplanations.b: RPE is the last resort; a WEL breach requires reducing exposure through higher-order controls, not continued reliance on masks.
distractorExplanations.c: Both the 8-hour TWA and the 15-minute STEL are legal limits; exceeding either one requires action to reduce exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: A WEL exceedance is not a notifiable event in itself; the legal duty is to reduce exposure using the hierarchy of control.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: WELs are legal maximums; exceedance triggers review and stronger controls to reduce exposure. Exposure monitoring may be required to confirm the reduction has worked.

options.a: Fire exits locked during cleaning, with keys held by the cleaner for emergencies
options.b: Lone worker check-in system, lighting, safe chemical use training, and access to toilets
options.c: Chemicals decanted into spray bottles by the cleaner, with the SDS file kept at head office
options.d: A panic alarm linked to the police, with breaks taken at the end of the shift

distractorExplanations.a: Fire exits must be openable without a key whenever people are inside; locking them compromises escape.
distractorExplanations.c: Decanted containers need labels and the SDS must be accessible on site; keeping it at head office fails hazard information duties.
distractorExplanations.d: Pushing breaks to shift end increases fatigue, and a panic alarm cannot help a cleaner who is injured and unable to press it.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Lone cleaning combines chemical COSHH, STF in dim areas, and welfare — fire exits must remain usable. Toilets should be on site so the cleaner does not need to leave the building.

options.a: Hose the spill into the bund drain with plenty of water to dilute the acid quickly
options.b: Leave the spill in the bund for collection next week, as the bund contains it
options.c: PPE, spill kit use, neutralise or absorb per procedure, and dispose as hazardous waste
options.d: Absorb with sawdust and place it in the general waste skip once it has dried out overnight

distractorExplanations.a: Adding water to concentrated acid can cause violent heat and splashing, and bund contents must not be released to drains untreated.
distractorExplanations.b: Bunds are secondary containment, not storage; spilled acid can corrode the bund and release fumes, so it must be cleared promptly.
distractorExplanations.d: Sawdust is combustible and can react with some acids, and acid-contaminated absorbent is hazardous waste, not general waste.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Chemical spills need trained response, containment, safe neutralisation/absorption, and waste disposal per SDS. Ventilate the store and investigate the cause once the spill is controlled.

options.a: The injured worker's supervisor, who should record the trip in the site accident book first
options.b: The cabin hire company, as supplier of the welfare units placed on site
options.c: The client's insurer, who must inspect the site before any repairs are made
options.d: The employer/main contractor coordinating site housekeeping and ground maintenance

distractorExplanations.a: Recording the accident is required but does not fix the paving; the duty to maintain traffic routes lies with the employer or main contractor.
distractorExplanations.b: The hire firm supplies cabins but does not control the ground between them; site layout and maintenance are the principal contractor's duty.
distractorExplanations.c: Insurers may investigate claims but have no duty to control site hazards, and repairs should not wait for them.

options.a: Not proceed until a competent person completes erection and issues positive inspection
options.b: Proceed on the completed lower lifts if the scaffold supervisor gives verbal approval
options.c: Proceed if workers wear harnesses clipped to the scaffold tubes while erection is finished
options.d: Proceed once the scaffold is visually checked by the trade foreman using it

distractorExplanations.b: An incomplete scaffold should be tagged out; verbal approval does not replace a completed inspection and a positive tag.
distractorExplanations.c: Harnesses do not make an incomplete structure safe, and incomplete scaffold may not be designed to take fall-arrest loads.
distractorExplanations.d: Inspection must be by a competent person after erection is complete, not a quick look by the user's own foreman.

options.a: Storing water at 30-35 °C in tanks so it is comfortable for welfare washing
options.b: Avoiding stagnant water, temperature control, and flushing
options.c: Chlorinating the system once at installation, then using it without further checks
options.d: Testing drinking water for E. coli monthly as the main Legionella control

distractorExplanations.a: 20-45 °C is the Legionella growth range; hot water should be stored at 60 °C and cold water kept below 20 °C.
distractorExplanations.c: One-off disinfection does not prevent regrowth; water systems need ongoing monitoring, flushing and temperature checks.
distractorExplanations.d: E. coli testing indicates faecal contamination, not Legionella; control relies on temperature, flushing and avoiding stagnation.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Stagnant warm water supports Legionella; site welfare tanks and hoses need management like permanent systems. Competent management of the water system oversees these controls.

options.a: Entering without a harness, although isolating the auger is optional for a short task
options.b: Working alone without a radio, though the energised auger poses little extra risk to the farmer
options.c: Confined space engulfment/mechanical hazards without isolation, atmosphere test, and permit
options.d: Failing to wear a dust mask, since grain dust is the main hazard in silo entry

distractorExplanations.a: Isolation of the auger is essential, not optional; contact with a running auger causes amputations and fatal injuries.
distractorExplanations.b: The energised auger is a critical mechanical hazard; lone working is one error but not the most serious one here.
distractorExplanations.d: Grain dust is a hazard, but engulfment and the running auger are the fatal risks, and a dust mask controls neither.

options.a: Section on exposure controls and personal protective equipment only
options.b: Section on stability and reactivity of the substance
options.c: Section on toxicological information and health effects
options.d: Section on accidental release measures and fire-fighting measures

distractorExplanations.a: Section 8 gives exposure limits and PPE but not the containment and clean-up method; that is Section 6, accidental release measures.
distractorExplanations.b: Section 10 covers reactivity and incompatible materials but not spill containment and clean-up, which sit in Section 6.
distractorExplanations.c: Section 11 describes health effects for medical and assessment use, not the practical spill response steps.

options.a: Using marked crawl boards, barriers, or alternative access avoiding the fragile panel
options.b: Walking only on the skylight frame, which is designed to bear a person's weight
options.c: Wearing a harness and lanyard attached to the skylight frame as an anchor point
options.d: Placing a warning sign beside the skylight and briefing workers about it at the toolbox talk

distractorExplanations.b: Skylight frames and upstands are not designed as walkways; fragile surfaces need covers, barriers or avoidance.
distractorExplanations.c: A skylight frame is not a rated anchor and can fail with the panel; collective protection should come first.
distractorExplanations.d: Signs and briefings are administrative controls that do not physically prevent a fall through the fragile panel.

options.a: Compacting sharps waste in yellow bags to reduce volume before collection
options.b: No hand contact, sharps container, and incident reporting for potential BBV exposure
options.c: Wearing gloves to handle sharps, with reporting needed if the skin is visibly bleeding
options.d: Hepatitis B vaccination, after which minor needlestick injuries need no follow-up

distractorExplanations.a: Sharps go in rigid puncture-resistant containers; compressing bags drives needles through and causes needlestick injuries.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves do not stop needle penetration, and any percutaneous exposure must be reported for post-exposure assessment, bleeding or not.
distractorExplanations.d: Vaccination does not protect against HIV or hepatitis C, so every needlestick still needs reporting and medical assessment.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Sharps and bloodborne virus risk need segregation, PPE, and post-exposure protocols. Training on biological routes of entry supports these controls.

options.a: Replacing individual COSHH assessments with a single site-wide hazard register
options.b: Recording the WEL for every substance so that air monitoring is no longer required
options.c: Listing substances used, locations, quantities, and linking to assessments and SDS
options.d: Showing the regulator which substances are exempt from labelling requirements

distractorExplanations.a: An inventory supports but does not replace substance- and task-specific assessments of how exposure occurs.
distractorExplanations.b: Listing WELs does not show actual exposure; monitoring may still be needed to confirm controls are effective.
distractorExplanations.d: Inventories list what is held and where; they do not create labelling exemptions, and hazardous substances must stay labelled.

options.a: Taping cables flat across doorways, which removes the trip risk at busy points
options.b: Coiling surplus cable on the floor beside the bench to keep it out of the way
options.c: Yellow-and-black hazard tape on the floor marking where cables cross walkways
options.d: Overhead routing, cable covers in walkways, and cordless tools where feasible

distractorExplanations.a: Taped cables across doorways still create a raised edge and wear quickly; cables should be routed overhead or away from routes.
distractorExplanations.b: Loose coils on the floor remain trip hazards and can overheat under load; surplus cable should be managed on reels or hooks.
distractorExplanations.c: Floor marking warns of the hazard but leaves the cable in the walking route; covers or rerouting remove it.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Cable management is a standard STF control in workshops and events. Housekeeping rules keep routes clear of loose cable.

options.a: High-risk tasks prohibited alone, check-in intervals, and escalation if contact lost
options.b: A mobile phone for each lone worker, with contact made when the worker needs help
options.c: Lone working permitted for all tasks provided the worker has five years' experience
options.d: Check-ins at the start and end of each shift, with escalation the next working day

distractorExplanations.b: Worker-initiated contact fails if the person is unconscious; policies need scheduled check-ins and escalation.
distractorExplanations.c: Experience does not make high-risk tasks such as confined space entry safe alone; some work must be prohibited for lone workers.
distractorExplanations.d: Next-day escalation is far too slow; lost contact must trigger an immediate response during the shift.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Policies set prohibited tasks, communication, and emergency escalation for lone workers. The policy should also define training for lone workers.

options.a: The examination certifies that workers' exposure is below the WEL for that year
options.b: Performance can degrade invisibly while workers believe they are protected
options.c: It replaces the need for daily operator checks of the airflow indicator
options.d: It is needed to confirm the fan motor meets electrical safety standards

distractorExplanations.a: Thorough examination checks LEV performance such as airflow and capture; it does not measure personal exposure or certify WEL compliance.
distractorExplanations.c: Statutory examination at intervals complements, not replaces, routine user checks such as airflow indicators.
distractorExplanations.d: Electrical safety of the fan is a separate inspection; LEV examination tests capture and airflow performance.

options.a: The task takes less than half a day and the ladder is footed by a second worker throughout
options.b: The work involves carrying heavy materials and both hands are needed for the task
options.c: Risk assessment shows low duration/light work and ladders are secured and inspected
options.d: A scaffold is available but the ladder is quicker to set up for a full-day task

distractorExplanations.a: HSE guidance suggests ladders for short-duration work of about 30 minutes; half a day is too long, and footing alone does not justify use.
distractorExplanations.b: Ladders suit light work with a handhold available; heavy loads or two-handed work need a platform such as a tower or MEWP.
distractorExplanations.d: Convenience does not justify ladders for prolonged work; a full day's task warrants a scaffold or other working platform.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Ladders are for short-duration light work where risk assessment justifies; misuse as platforms or overcrowding is unsafe. Ladders should also be used by trained staff.

options.a: Toilets and drinking water, with meals eaten at the work face to limit walking
options.b: Changing rooms and lockers, with a shared towel provided at the washing point
options.c: Drinking water and toilets, with hand washing provided once dust levels are measured
options.d: Dusty work requiring washing, potable water, and separate clean eating space

distractorExplanations.a: Eating at the work face allows dust ingestion; demolition sites need clean rest and eating areas away from contamination.
distractorExplanations.b: Shared towels spread contamination; hand drying should use disposable towels or dryers.
distractorExplanations.c: Washing facilities are needed from the start of dusty demolition work, not after monitoring confirms exposure.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Demolition welfare must address dust, noise, hydration, and hygiene with maintained facilities. Rest areas away from noise are also needed on demolition sites.

options.a: Absorb with appropriate kit, disinfect per protocol, PPE, and waste segregation
options.b: Mop up with detergent and hot water, then return the mop to general use
options.c: Cover with paper towels and leave it for the night cleaning team to deal with later
options.d: Disinfect with alcohol hand gel, then place waste in the domestic waste stream

distractorExplanations.b: Detergent cleans but does not disinfect, and a contaminated mop spreads pathogens; spill kits with disinfectant and disposal are needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Biological spills must be dealt with promptly by trained staff; leaving them exposes others and delays disinfection.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand gel is not a surface spill disinfectant, and contaminated material must go to clinical waste, not domestic waste.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Biological spill procedures protect staff and others via disinfectant, PPE, and clinical waste routes. Staff exposure should then be reviewed.

options.a: Replacing respiratory protection with LEV so that exposure is controlled at source
options.b: Replacing a hazardous substance or process with a less hazardous one
options.c: Rotating workers between tasks so that each person's exposure time is reduced
options.d: Switching to a different supplier's version of the same substance at lower cost

distractorExplanations.a: Moving from RPE to LEV upgrades to an engineering control; substitution changes the substance or process itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Job rotation is an administrative control limiting duration; substitution replaces the hazardous substance or process.
distractorExplanations.d: The same substance from another supplier carries the same hazard; substitution requires a less hazardous alternative.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Substitution is high in COSHH hierarchy — less hazardous products or processes reduce exposure potential. The duty applies where substitution is reasonably practicable.

options.a: Painted yellow lines at the edge, with pallets allowed to overhang for forklift access
options.b: Harnesses for staff on the mezzanine, with pallets stacked up to the open edge
options.c: Edge protection, pallet placement rules, signage, and supervision of loading activity
options.d: Signage below the mezzanine, with loading gates left open during busy periods

distractorExplanations.a: Painted lines warn but do not prevent falls or dropped loads; overhanging pallets need physical edge protection.
distractorExplanations.b: Personal fall protection ranks below collective edge protection, and stacking to the edge still risks falling loads.
distractorExplanations.d: Open loading gates remove the edge protection; gates should be interlocked up-and-over types so the edge is not exposed.

options.a: Static air sampling at the booth door once a year to confirm the LEV is still capturing mist
options.b: Face-fit testing of the operator's RPE as a measure of personal exposure
options.c: Lung function testing only, since symptoms show whether exposure is too high
options.d: Air sampling, biological monitoring where appropriate, and comparison with WEL

distractorExplanations.a: A static sample at the door does not represent breathing-zone exposure, and LEV checks are separate from exposure monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Face-fit testing confirms the mask seals; it does not measure the isocyanate concentration workers are exposed to.
distractorExplanations.c: Lung function testing is health surveillance that detects harm after it occurs; it does not quantify exposure.

options.a: Grease on floors, wet surfaces, poor footwear policy, and inadequate cleaning schedule
options.b: Slip-resistant flooring, prompt spill clean-up, and a non-slip footwear policy
options.c: Regular degreasing, maintained grease traps, and drainage channels at the cooking line
options.d: Dry-mopping spills during service and placing absorbent mats near the fryers

distractorExplanations.b: These are the standard kitchen slip controls; they reduce slip risk rather than increase it.
distractorExplanations.c: Degreasing, maintained traps and drainage remove contamination from floors, so they lower slip risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Prompt dry mopping and absorbent mats remove wet and greasy contamination, reducing rather than increasing slips.

options.a: That the entrants have signed the permit and the task description section is complete
options.b: Isolation, atmospheric tests, rescue arrangements, and competence before signing
options.c: Gas test results from the previous shift, if the space was closed overnight
options.d: That the standby person will enter first to check the atmosphere is safe

distractorExplanations.a: Signatures and paperwork are not enough; the issuer must verify physical precautions such as isolation and gas test results.
distractorExplanations.c: Atmospheres can change while a space is closed; tests must be current, immediately before entry, not from the previous shift.
distractorExplanations.d: Nobody should enter to check the atmosphere; testing is done from outside with a calibrated detector before entry.

options.a: A uniform and ID badge, with visit details kept in the van for the engineer's reference
options.b: Visits booked without appointments so tenants cannot plan confrontations
options.c: Lone worker traceability, violence/assault awareness, and mobile communication
options.d: Double-staffing every visit as a blanket rule instead of assessing each address

distractorExplanations.a: Details held in the van give no traceability; the employer needs a system to know where the engineer is and when they are due back.
distractorExplanations.b: Unannounced visits increase surprise and conflict; appointments with ID checks improve predictability and safety.
distractorExplanations.d: Blanket double-staffing is disproportionate and ignores risk assessment; flagged addresses can be double-staffed while others use traceability.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Domestic lone work faces variable environments and violence risk; traceability and training are key. Safe entry procedures for tenants' homes complete the controls.

options.a: Fire-rated cabinet with oxidisers on the lower shelf to keep them apart from solvents
options.b: Sealed, unventilated cupboard to stop vapour escaping into the workshop
options.c: Any quantity in a fire-rated cabinet, provided it is at least 1 m from welding
options.d: Ventilated, fire-rated store, quantity limits, and segregation from oxidisers

distractorExplanations.a: Oxidisers in the same cabinet, even on another shelf, are not segregated; they intensify fires and need separate storage.
distractorExplanations.b: Unventilated storage lets flammable vapour build up inside; flammable stores need ventilation to prevent an explosive atmosphere.
distractorExplanations.c: Workroom quantity limits apply (for example 50 litres of highly flammable liquid), and 1 m is far too close to hot work sparks.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Flammable storage needs rated cabinets/rooms, segregation, ventilation, and ignition source control. Ignition sources must also be kept away from the store.

options.a: Be planned before work starts, with trained personnel and equipment
options.b: Rely on calling the emergency services, who will reach the worker within minutes
options.c: Be written after the first suspension incident so it reflects real site conditions
options.d: Rely on the worker's lanyard holding them until the end of the shift

distractorExplanations.b: Emergency service response may be too slow for suspension trauma; employers need their own planned rescue, not reliance on a call-out.
distractorExplanations.c: Rescue plans must exist before work begins; waiting for an incident leaves a suspended worker without help.
distractorExplanations.d: Suspension in a harness can cause suspension trauma within minutes; prompt rescue is required, not waiting.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Rescue plans address suspension trauma and timely recovery — required in work at height planning. Rescue equipment must suit the suspension scenario to limit suspension trauma.

options.a: Musculoskeletal disorders from repetitive assembly-line tasks
options.b: Slips, trips, fires, and struck-by incidents from clutter and waste
options.c: Noise-induced hearing loss from machinery operating nearby
options.d: Occupational dermatitis from contact with cutting fluids

distractorExplanations.a: Repetitive task MSDs are ergonomic issues controlled by workstation design and rotation, not housekeeping.
distractorExplanations.c: Noise exposure is controlled at source and by hearing protection; floor tidiness does not change noise levels.
distractorExplanations.d: Dermatitis is controlled through substitution, gloves and skin care, not general floor housekeeping.

options.a: Recapping needles with both hands before placing them in yellow clinical waste bags
options.b: Thick gauntlet gloves for porters so that needlestick injuries cannot occur
options.c: Sharps containers at point of use, training, and post-exposure prophylaxis pathway
options.d: Reporting only injuries that draw blood, with first aid as the main response

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injury, and sharps belong in rigid containers, not bags.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves reduce but do not prevent needle penetration; sharps must be disposed of at the point of use.
distractorExplanations.d: Every needlestick needs reporting and urgent medical assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis, whether or not blood is drawn.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Needlestick protocols emphasise no recapping, sharps bins, and rapid medical assessment. Prompt reporting of every needlestick triggers that pathway.

options.a: Measuring the dust concentration in the operator's breathing zone
options.b: Recording the date of the last statutory thorough examination
options.c: Indicating the noise level produced by the extraction fan
options.d: Showing whether airflow is adequate before starting dusty work

distractorExplanations.a: An airflow indicator shows hood or duct airflow, not personal dust exposure, which needs air sampling.
distractorExplanations.b: The examination date is shown on a label or record; the gauge shows current airflow performance.
distractorExplanations.c: Airflow indicators measure air movement or pressure, not fan noise, which needs a sound level meter.

options.a: Do not proceed until higher-order controls are implemented or work method changed
options.b: Proceed if workers wear harnesses attached to the roof structure and are supervised
options.c: Proceed after a toolbox talk on fragile roofs, as workers will be aware of the risk
options.d: Proceed if the work takes less than 30 minutes and the weather is dry

distractorExplanations.b: PPE and supervision are lower-order controls; fragile roofs without edge protection need collective measures first.
distractorExplanations.c: Awareness training is an administrative control; it does not stop a fall through fragile material.
distractorExplanations.d: Short duration does not reduce the consequence of a fall through a fragile roof; edge protection is still needed.

options.a: Drinking water points beside the process line so workers need not leave their stations
options.b: Providing hydration, cool rest areas, and maintained toilets away from the process
options.c: Extra shifts and fewer breaks in hot weather to finish production before peak heat
options.d: Rest areas inside the process hall so supervisors can recall workers quickly

distractorExplanations.a: Water near corrosive process zones risks contamination and ingestion; welfare must be separated from the hazard.
distractorExplanations.c: Reducing breaks increases heat stress; hot process work needs rest, hydration and a heat plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Rest areas in the hot, chemical-contaminated hall give no recovery from heat and allow contamination of food and drink.

nebosh-readiness-check-agents-workplace-.explanation: Welfare must be accessible and hygienic, separated from chemical process zones. Chemical hygiene such as washing and decontamination also forms part of welfare provision.

options.a: Equipment is suitable, maintained, and used only by trained/competent people
options.b: Equipment carries a CE/UKCA mark, so no further suitability assessment is needed
options.c: Equipment is inspected annually by the supplier, with maintenance left to users
options.d: Equipment is guarded, with training given to new starters in their first year

distractorExplanations.b: A conformity mark shows the manufacturer's compliance, but the employer must still assess suitability for the specific task and environment.
distractorExplanations.c: Inspection frequency is risk-based, and maintenance is the employer's duty, not something to leave to individual users.
distractorExplanations.d: Guarding is one PUWER duty, but training must be given to every user as needed, not just to new starters.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: PUWER requires suitable equipment, maintenance, inspection, and competent use with effective controls. Inspection is also required where deterioration could cause danger.

options.a: Failure to carry out the daily pre-use inspection of the press
options.b: Failure to prevent access to dangerous parts during operation
options.c: Failure to provide adequate lighting at the drilling station
options.d: Failure to mark the controls clearly for the operator

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-use checks matter, but removing the guard is a failure of the duty to prevent access to dangerous parts.
distractorExplanations.c: Lighting is a separate PUWER requirement; removing the guard relates to access to dangerous parts of machinery.
distractorExplanations.d: Marking of controls is a separate duty; removing the chuck guard breaches the dangerous-parts requirement.

options.a: Check the load is within 110% of SWL and the crane's annual test is valid
options.b: Check the slings, then guide the load by hand from beneath as it is raised
options.c: Check SWL, slings, hooks, brakes, and lifting plan including exclusion zone
options.d: Check the crane's thorough examination report is in date and start the lift

distractorExplanations.a: The SWL must not be exceeded at all; there is no 10% tolerance, and a valid test certificate does not replace pre-lift checks.
distractorExplanations.b: Nobody should stand under a suspended load; tag lines are used to steady loads from a safe position.
distractorExplanations.d: A valid examination record is necessary but not sufficient; slings, hooks and the lift plan must be checked before each lift.

options.a: Electric shock from damaged wiring on the drive motor
options.b: Noise exposure from the belt running during servicing
options.c: Manual handling injury from lifting replacement rollers
options.d: Unexpected start-up causing entanglement or crushing

distractorExplanations.a: Shock is possible, but an unisolated conveyor is mainly a risk of unexpected start-up and entanglement in moving parts.
distractorExplanations.b: Noise is secondary; the critical risk without lock-off is someone restarting the conveyor while the fitter is inside the danger zone.
distractorExplanations.c: Manual handling may apply, but the absence of isolation creates the fatal risk of unexpected start-up.

options.a: Fuel, oxygen (or oxidiser), and heat (ignition source)
options.b: Fuel, oxygen, heat, and an uninhibited chemical chain reaction
options.c: Smoke, flame, and heat produced during combustion
options.d: Fuel, carbon dioxide, and an ignition source

distractorExplanations.b: Adding the chemical chain reaction describes the four-element fire tetrahedron, not the three-sided fire triangle.
distractorExplanations.c: These are products of combustion, not the three conditions needed for a fire to start and continue.
distractorExplanations.d: CO2 is an extinguishing agent that displaces oxygen; oxygen, not carbon dioxide, is the second side of the triangle.

options.a: Directly outside the main entrance so the roll call can be taken quickly
options.b: In the car park beside the LPG and fuel store, where there is the most open space available
options.c: Clearly signed, away from building entrances, and known to all occupants from induction
options.d: Varied for each drill so staff learn to find the nearest safe location

distractorExplanations.a: Assembly points next to exits expose evacuees to smoke and falling debris and obstruct firefighters' access.
distractorExplanations.b: Open space helps, but a fuel store nearby risks fire spread and explosion close to the evacuees.
distractorExplanations.d: Changing assembly points causes confusion and undermines roll call; occupants must know one consistent location.

options.a: Supply voltage rating alone, independent of body resistance or contact time
options.b: Whether the supply is DC, which is more dangerous than AC at the same voltage
options.c: The fuse rating of the circuit, since a lower fuse prevents a lethal shock
options.d: Current path through the body, magnitude, duration, and frequency (for AC)

distractorExplanations.a: Voltage drives current, but severity depends on the current that flows, its path and duration, which depend on body resistance.
distractorExplanations.b: AC at 50-60 Hz is generally more dangerous than DC at the same voltage because it causes muscle tetany and fibrillation.
distractorExplanations.c: Fuses protect cables from overcurrent and blow at currents far above lethal body currents of around 50 mA; they do not prevent shock.

options.a: Isolate, lock-off, test dead, and earth if required before work
options.b: Test dead, isolate, lock-off, then begin work on the motor circuit
options.c: Isolate at the switch, check the label, and start work if it reads OFF
options.d: Isolate and fit a warning tag, then start work without a padlock fitted

distractorExplanations.b: Testing before isolating proves nothing; the circuit must be isolated and locked off first, then proved dead.
distractorExplanations.c: Switch labels can be wrong or the circuit fed from elsewhere; conductors must be proved dead with an approved tester.
distractorExplanations.d: Tags alone can be ignored or removed; the isolation must be locked off and proved dead before work starts.

options.a: Replace user visual checks with an annual electrical test of every appliance
options.b: Maintain portable electrical equipment in safe condition through inspection and testing
options.c: Certify each appliance as safe until the next scheduled test date
options.d: Test fixed electrical installations such as distribution boards, sockets and fixed wiring

distractorExplanations.a: Most faults are found by user visual checks; PAT complements them, and test frequency is risk-based rather than a fixed annual test.
distractorExplanations.c: A pass label shows condition on the test date; damage can occur at any time, so pre-use checks remain essential.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixed installations are covered by periodic inspection of the installation, not by portable appliance testing.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: PAT complements user checks and maintenance; frequency depends on environment and equipment type. Faulty items are repaired or replaced before reuse.

options.a: Overcurrent from overloaded circuits that could overheat cables
options.b: Voltage surges from lightning strikes that could damage connected electronic equipment
options.c: Earth leakage currents that could cause electric shock and some fire risks
options.d: Short circuits between live and neutral conductors in the cable

distractorExplanations.a: Overcurrent protection is the role of fuses and MCBs; an RCD detects imbalance between live and neutral.
distractorExplanations.b: Surge protection devices handle transient overvoltages; RCDs respond to earth leakage current.
distractorExplanations.d: A live-neutral short creates no imbalance, so an RCD may not trip; fuses or MCBs clear short circuits.

options.a: It warns the operator with an alarm before the chuck starts
options.b: It contains swarf and coolant so the floor stays clean
options.c: It replaces the need for isolation during maintenance work
options.d: It prevents access to dangerous parts while they are moving

distractorExplanations.a: Warnings do not prevent contact; an interlock stops motion when the guard is opened.
distractorExplanations.b: Containing swarf is a side benefit of an enclosure; the interlock's purpose is to stop motion whenever access is possible.
distractorExplanations.c: Interlocks protect routine access during operation; maintenance still requires isolation and lock-off.

options.a: Wear, deformation, and hidden damage can cause catastrophic failure at SWL
options.b: Chain slings must be re-rated to a lower SWL each year of service
options.c: It replaces the need for a visual check by the slinger before each lift is made
options.d: The examination certificate is needed to calculate the load's weight

distractorExplanations.b: Slings are not progressively de-rated by age; examination finds defects that require repair or withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.c: Thorough examination supplements, not replaces, the pre-use checks made by the person rigging the load.
distractorExplanations.d: Certificates confirm the accessory is safe at its SWL; they do not determine the weight of the load.

options.a: Exposure to welding fume and the need for LEV and RPE
options.b: Ignition sources near combustibles during welding, cutting, or grinding
options.c: Electrical isolation and lock-off of plant before mechanical maintenance work
options.d: Entry into tanks and pits with hazardous atmospheres

distractorExplanations.a: Fume exposure is managed through a hazardous substance assessment; hot work permits control fire risk from sparks and heat.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolation is controlled by an electrical or mechanical isolation permit, not a hot work permit.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the role of a confined space entry permit, although hot work inside a confined space may need both permits.

options.a: Removing the need for guards because the machine cannot move
options.b: Exempting the machine from periodic inspection because it is classed as fixed plant
options.c: Reducing unexpected movement that could alter guarding effectiveness or stability
options.d: Allowing it to be run at higher speed than the maker's rating

distractorExplanations.a: Fixing the base does not guard moving parts; dangerous parts still need guards.
distractorExplanations.b: Fixed equipment is still subject to inspection and maintenance where deterioration could cause danger.
distractorExplanations.d: Stability does not justify exceeding the manufacturer's speed rating; that would need reassessment and the maker's approval.

options.a: CO2 cools the fire rapidly to below the auto-ignition point
options.b: CO2 can be used safely in confined switchrooms with occupants present
options.c: CO2 forms a foam film that seals the surface of burning cables
options.d: CO2 is non-conductive and leaves no residue on sensitive equipment

distractorExplanations.a: CO2 works mainly by displacing oxygen (smothering); its cooling effect is limited and re-ignition is possible.
distractorExplanations.b: CO2 displaces oxygen and can asphyxiate occupants in small enclosed rooms; ventilate and leave after discharge.
distractorExplanations.c: Film-forming is how AFFF foam works on liquid fires; CO2 is a gas that smothers without a film or residue.

options.a: Keep hands clear of the closing die during the stroke
options.b: Allow two operators to share the press workload safely
options.c: Prevent the press cycling faster than its rated speed
options.d: Replace the need for side guards on the press brake

distractorExplanations.b: Two-hand controls are designed for one operator using both hands; they are not a workload-sharing device.
distractorExplanations.c: Speed limiting is a separate control function; two-hand control keeps the operator's hands out of the danger zone.
distractorExplanations.d: Two-hand controls protect the operator but not others nearby; side and rear guarding is still needed.

options.a: Structural stability issue requiring a load-bearing review
options.b: Fuel and ignition pathway issue requiring material selection
options.c: Means of escape issue solved by adding extra exit signage
options.d: Fire detection issue solved by adding smoke alarms inside flats

distractorExplanations.a: Combustible cladding is a fire-spread problem; structural load-bearing capacity is not the main concern.
distractorExplanations.c: Signage helps occupants find exits but does nothing to stop flame spread up the facade.
distractorExplanations.d: Detection gives warning but does not stop external flame spread, which depends on cladding materials and cavity barriers.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: External fire spread involves fuel continuity and ignition — fire safety strategy and materials matter. Compartmentation and cavity barriers should also be reviewed.

options.a: The job description and the electrician's signature on completion
options.b: The cost code, contractor company name, and estimated duration of the electrical work
options.c: Points isolated, locks applied, tester identity, time, and handback procedure
options.d: The circuit drawing number and the date of the last PAT test

distractorExplanations.a: A description and sign-off are part of a permit, but it must also record isolation points, locks and test results.
distractorExplanations.b: Administrative details do not ensure safety; the permit must record where isolation was made and how it was proved dead.
distractorExplanations.d: PAT dates concern portable appliances, not the isolation of a fixed circuit for maintenance.

options.a: Acceptable if the cage is securely chained to the forks and the operator stays in the cab
options.b: Acceptable for short tasks under 15 minutes if workers wear harnesses
options.c: Preferred over a scissor lift because the forklift is already on site
options.d: Generally prohibited or highly restricted because it is not designed for personnel lift

distractorExplanations.a: A non-integrated cage chained to forks is not designed for lifting people; integrated platforms with proper controls are required.
distractorExplanations.b: Short duration and harnesses do not turn a materials-handling truck into a safe people lifter.
distractorExplanations.c: Convenience does not override suitability; a MEWP designed for lifting people is the correct equipment.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Forklifts are primarily for materials; personnel elevation needs designed work platforms and risk assessment. A proper MEWP or integrated work platform should be used instead.

options.a: Illuminate paths when normal lighting fails, supporting safe evacuation
options.b: Operate for at least 10 minutes after a mains failure
options.c: Light only the final exit doors so occupants can find them
options.d: Switch on when the fire alarm sounds, powered independently of the mains supply

distractorExplanations.b: Escape route emergency lighting is typically rated for 1 to 3 hours, not 10 minutes.
distractorExplanations.c: Escape route lighting must cover the whole route, changes of direction and stairs, not just the final exits.
distractorExplanations.d: Emergency lighting responds to failure of normal lighting, not alarm activation; the two are separate systems.

options.a: Insulated gloves and tools, with live work as the normal method for switchgear
options.b: De-energising, arc-rated PPE if live work unavoidable, and remote racking where possible
options.c: Standard cotton overalls and safety glasses, with the panel door kept open for visibility
options.d: Earthing the panel frame so that any arc is conducted safely to ground

distractorExplanations.a: Insulated gloves protect against shock, not arc flash heat, and live work should be the exception rather than the norm.
distractorExplanations.c: Ordinary clothing can ignite in an arc flash; arc-rated clothing and face protection are needed if live work is justified.
distractorExplanations.d: Earthing protects against indirect shock but does not prevent or contain the energy released in an arc flash.

options.a: Pressure gauge reading at start-up and the vessel's paint condition
options.b: The vessel's original CE mark and purchase date as recorded by the equipment supplier
options.c: Guards, safety valves, mounting integrity, and compliance with written scheme
options.d: Operator training records and the noise level near the vessel

distractorExplanations.a: Gauge and paint checks are routine observations, not an inspection of safety valves and mounting integrity.
distractorExplanations.b: Conformity marking and age do not confirm current safe condition; in-service inspection checks safety devices and mountings.
distractorExplanations.d: Training and noise matter elsewhere, but this inspection concerns safety valves, guards and mountings.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Pressure systems need integrity of mountings, safety devices, and statutory examination schemes. A written scheme of examination applies where the pressure system requires one.

options.a: Fighting the fire with the nearest extinguisher before raising the alarm
options.b: Collecting the visitor book and personal belongings before leaving the floor area
options.c: Re-entering the building to check toilets after reaching the assembly point
options.d: Sweeping assigned areas, assisting mobility-impaired persons, reporting status

distractorExplanations.a: The alarm is raised first; wardens tackle a fire only if trained and it is safe, not before evacuation starts.
distractorExplanations.b: Visitor lists help roll call, but collecting belongings delays evacuation.
distractorExplanations.c: Sweeps are done on the way out; re-entry into a burning building is left to the fire service.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Wardens support orderly evacuation and area clearance; firefighting is only if trained and safe within role. Status is reported to the evacuation coordinator.

options.a: Overheating the cable due to reduced heat dissipation
options.b: Tripping the RCD due to earth leakage from the coiled turns
options.c: Blowing the plug fuse because coiling raises the current drawn
options.d: Voltage drop that makes the heater run cooler and less efficiently

distractorExplanations.b: Coiling does not create earth leakage; the danger is the cable overheating under a high-current load such as a heater.
distractorExplanations.c: Coiling does not increase the current the heater draws; heat builds up because it cannot dissipate from the coils.
distractorExplanations.d: Voltage drop on a short lead is minor; the real hazard is heat build-up in the coiled cable.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Coiled cables can overheat under load, creating ignition sources — common PAT/ electricity scenario. Heat cannot escape from tightly packed coils, so insulation can soften, melt and ignite.

options.a: Electrical isolation of the pump motor, with the ram left raised on hydraulic pressure
options.b: Isolation of energy, blocking/supporting ram, bleed pressure, and controlled reinstatement
options.c: Lowering the ram fully, then working with guards removed while the pump runs
options.d: Bleeding pressure via the relief valve, then restarting the pump to check the seals for leaks

distractorExplanations.a: Isolating the motor leaves stored hydraulic pressure; the ram must be blocked and pressure bled down.
distractorExplanations.c: Running the pump with guards removed exposes the fitter to moving parts; isolation and blocking are needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Bleeding pressure is one step, but the ram must also be blocked and energy isolated; restarting during access is unsafe.

options.a: Lower the load slightly and continue, as the indicator allows a 10% margin
options.b: Ask the slinger to confirm the load weight by radio and then continue with the lift
options.c: Override the indicator once, then report it to the appointed person
options.d: Stop the lift, reassess load weight and rigging, and not override safety device

distractorExplanations.a: Overload indicators signal that rated capacity is reached or exceeded; there is no allowance to continue the lift.
distractorExplanations.b: Verbal confirmation does not override the safety device; the lift must stop and the load and rigging be reassessed.
distractorExplanations.c: Safety devices must not be overridden; reporting afterwards does not make the overloaded lift safe.

options.a: Systems constructed, maintained, and used to prevent danger
options.b: Live working by default where isolation would halt production
options.c: PAT testing of every appliance at fixed annual intervals
options.d: Certification of all electricians by a government licence

distractorExplanations.b: Live work is permitted only when it is unreasonable to make dead and risks are controlled; lost production alone does not justify it.
distractorExplanations.c: The regulations require maintenance to prevent danger; they do not prescribe annual PAT for every item.
distractorExplanations.d: The duty is competence to prevent danger; a specific government licence is not what the regulations require.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Prevent danger through design, maintenance, competence, and safe isolation — live work only when justified. Competence and safe isolation are required for work on electrical systems.

options.a: Operators need access several times per shift to clear product blockages from the roller
options.b: Access is infrequent and guard removal for maintenance can be planned with isolation
options.c: The roller is cleaned while running with a brush held by hand
options.d: The belt speed is low enough that a trip wire can stop it

distractorExplanations.a: Frequent access suits interlocked guards; fixed guards that must be removed often tend to be left off.
distractorExplanations.c: Cleaning while running exposes hands to the in-running nip; fixed guards and isolation are required.
distractorExplanations.d: Trip devices are a secondary measure; fixed guards suit infrequent access, whatever the belt speed.

options.a: Test each smoke detector with aerosol spray and confirm the panel registers it
options.b: Check the panel shows no faults and record it, without sounding the alarm
options.c: Trigger a call point and confirm alarm audibility at representative locations
options.d: Use the same call point each week so that results are comparable

distractorExplanations.a: Testing every detector is part of periodic servicing by a competent person; the weekly user test uses one call point.
distractorExplanations.b: A visual panel check does not prove sounders work; the weekly test must activate the alarm.
distractorExplanations.d: Call points are rotated so each is tested over time; using the same one leaves the others unchecked.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Weekly tests verify basic function; full servicing is periodic by competent person. A different call point or detector zone is used each week in rotation.

options.a: Wrap the damaged section with insulating tape and retest it later
options.b: Label it as faulty but leave it in use until a spare arrives
options.c: Fit a lower-rated fuse in the plug so it blows before a shock
options.d: Remove from service, repair or replace, and retest before return

distractorExplanations.a: Tape is not an acceptable repair for exposed conductors; the lead must be replaced or properly repaired first.
distractorExplanations.b: A failed item must be withdrawn immediately; a label alone does not stop people using it.
distractorExplanations.c: Fuses protect against overcurrent, not shock from exposed copper; the lead must be replaced.

options.a: Statutory intervals, examination scheme, and events like damage or overload
options.b: The manufacturer's annual service date, with no other events triggering an examination
options.c: A fixed 24-month interval for all lifting accessories
options.d: Operator pre-use checks, which replace periodic examination

distractorExplanations.b: LOLER intervals are 6 or 12 months or per an examination scheme, plus after damage or exceptional events.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifting accessories require thorough examination at least every 6 months, not every 24 months.
distractorExplanations.d: Pre-use checks support but do not replace thorough examination by a competent person.

options.a: Slip hazards only, as flour is not flammable once settled
options.b: Explosive atmospheres and deflagration if ignited with adequate concentration
options.c: Asphyxiation from airborne flour dust displacing oxygen inside the mill's silos
options.d: Class B fires that should be tackled with foam extinguishers

distractorExplanations.a: Settled flour can be raised into a cloud and cause secondary explosions; it is a combustible dust.
distractorExplanations.c: Flour dust does not displace oxygen like an inert gas; its main hazard is explosion when suspended and ignited.
distractorExplanations.d: Burning flour is a Class A solid; the key hazard is a dust explosion, not a flammable liquid fire.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Dust explosions need fuel-air mix, ignition, and confinement — process fire safety and housekeeping critical. Confinement of the dust cloud increases explosion pressure.

options.a: Switch the isolator off and fit a 'Do not operate' tag without a lock
options.b: Lock off and prove dead on the supply side before starting work
options.c: Lock in off position, prove dead on load side, and communicate with all affected workers
options.d: Lock in off position and keep the single key on the panel ready for the next shift to use

distractorExplanations.a: Tags alone can be removed or ignored; personal locks prevent re-energisation.
distractorExplanations.b: Proving dead must be done on the load side where work takes place; the supply side remains live.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving the key at the panel lets others remove the lock; each worker keeps their own key.

options.a: Grouped together on one central control panel serving the machines across the area
options.b: Identical in colour and shape across machines to simplify training
options.c: Located behind the guard so only trained staff can reach them
options.d: Clearly marked, positioned for safe operation, and not cause additional hazard

distractorExplanations.a: Central panels away from the machine cause confusion; controls must be positioned so the operator can see the danger zone.
distractorExplanations.b: Controls should be clearly identifiable by function; identical unlabelled controls lead to wrong operation.
distractorExplanations.c: Controls must be reachable from a safe operating position; hiding them behind guards delays stopping the machine.

options.a: Separating fuel surface from oxygen with foam blanket and cooling where applicable
options.b: Displacing oxygen from the room as the foam expands into a gas
options.c: Interrupting the chemical chain reaction within the flame zone
options.d: Diluting the solvent with the water in the foam so the mixture is no longer flammable

distractorExplanations.b: Foam blankets the liquid surface; displacing oxygen as a gas describes how CO2 extinguishers work.
distractorExplanations.c: Chain-reaction inhibition is how dry powder agents mainly work, not foam blanketing.
distractorExplanations.d: Foam floats on the fuel rather than diluting it, and many solvents stay flammable when mixed with water.

options.a: Chain tension and fuel level, with PPE needed only for felling work
options.b: Chain brake function, sharpness, guards, fuel system integrity, and PPE availability
options.c: Throttle response and chain oil, with the chain brake tested yearly
options.d: Engine start and idle speed, with the chain catcher removed if it is found to be damaged

distractorExplanations.a: Chainsaw PPE (leg, eye, hearing and head protection) is needed for all chainsaw use, not just felling.
distractorExplanations.c: The chain brake protects against kickback and must be checked before each use, not annually.
distractorExplanations.d: A damaged chain catcher must be replaced before use; removing it leaves no protection from a broken chain.

options.a: Be 230V with an RCD, since reduced voltage is needed only in wet areas
options.b: Be 230V Class I tools with the RCD bypassed if it trips repeatedly
options.c: Be 110V centre-tapped to earth where practicable and RCD protected
options.d: Be 400V three-phase to reduce current draw on long extension runs

distractorExplanations.a: 110V CTE is the preferred site supply because the maximum shock voltage to earth is 55V; it is not limited to wet areas.
distractorExplanations.b: Repeated trips indicate a fault that needs investigation; bypassing an RCD removes shock protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher voltage increases shock severity; reduced 110V supplies are used on site for portable tools.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Reduced voltage and RCD use lower shock risk on harsh sites; conditions demand robust inspection. Tools should also be visually checked before use.

options.a: Allow smoke to spread so detectors throughout trigger sooner
options.b: Contain the fire long enough for the building structure and contents to be saved
options.c: Replace the need for an evacuation plan in high-rise buildings
options.d: Limit fire and smoke spread, protecting escape routes and property

distractorExplanations.a: Compartmentation restricts smoke; detection works without needing smoke to spread through the building.
distractorExplanations.b: Property protection is a benefit, but the primary aim is life safety by protecting escape routes.
distractorExplanations.c: Even stay-put strategies rely on an evacuation plan; compartmentation supports it rather than replacing it.

options.a: Fixed or interlocked guard preventing access to the mesh zone
options.b: Warning signs and training while the gears run unguarded
options.c: A trip wire near the gears so operators can stop them
options.d: PPE such as close-fitting gloves for workers who reach near the gears

distractorExplanations.b: Signs and training are lower-order controls; in-running nips need physical guarding.
distractorExplanations.c: Trip devices stop the machine after contact may already have occurred; fixed or interlocked guards prevent access.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves can be drawn into nip points, increasing entanglement risk; guarding is required.

options.a: After a test run without guards confirms the repair was successful
options.b: Before power is restored and before operators resume production
options.c: At the end of the shift, once the backlog of production has cleared
options.d: Once the maintenance permit has been signed off the next day

distractorExplanations.a: Test runs without guards expose people to dangerous parts; guards are refitted before power is restored.
distractorExplanations.c: Running without guards to clear a backlog exposes operators; guards go back before production restarts.
distractorExplanations.d: Permit handback includes refitting guards before power is restored, not at a later date.

options.a: Insulating footwear and rubber mats to stop charge flowing to workers
options.b: Higher filling flow rates so less time is spent in the hazardous zone
options.c: Bonding and earthing, conductive footwear/floors, and exclusion of ignition sources
options.d: Plastic containers, since they cannot conduct electricity to create an igniting spark

distractorExplanations.a: Insulating footwear lets charge build up on the body; conductive footwear and floors dissipate it.
distractorExplanations.b: Higher flow velocity generates more static charge; flow rates are kept low during filling.
distractorExplanations.d: Insulating plastic containers accumulate charge and can discharge as a spark; conductive, bonded containers are used.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Bonding/earthing prevents static buildup discharges in flammable atmospheres. Humidity control can also reduce static build-up.

options.a: The crane's annual examination certificate and operator licence
options.b: The time the lift starts and the number of slingers available
options.c: Load weight and crane capacity, with wind speed checked after the lift is complete
options.d: Load weight, centre of gravity, crane capacity, wind, and exclusion zone

distractorExplanations.a: Certificates confirm equipment and competence, but a lift plan must address the load, capacity and conditions.
distractorExplanations.b: Scheduling and staffing are logistics; the plan must cover load weight, crane capacity and wind.
distractorExplanations.c: Wind limits must be checked before and during the lift; checking afterwards gives no protection.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Complex lifts need documented planning beyond routine simple lifts. The rigging arrangement and communication method are also planned.

options.a: Employer-appointed competent person or fire warden following procedure
options.b: The fire alarm maintenance contractor during each quarterly service visit
options.c: The local fire service, who test alarms on request each week
options.d: Each employee in turn, without a written procedure or record

distractorExplanations.b: Contractors service the system periodically; weekly user tests are done by the premises' own nominated person.
distractorExplanations.c: Fire services do not carry out routine weekly tests; that is the responsible person's duty.
distractorExplanations.d: Weekly tests follow a procedure and are logged by a nominated person, not done ad hoc by any employee.

options.a: Suitable for use in wet conditions without an RCD
options.b: No reliance on earth wire; basic plus supplementary insulation
options.c: The tool must be connected to an earthed plug to be safe
options.d: The tool is exempt from user checks and portable appliance testing

distractorExplanations.a: Class II reduces shock risk from internal faults but is not rated for wet conditions; RCD protection is still advisable.
distractorExplanations.c: Class II tools have no earth connection; safety comes from the double insulation layers.
distractorExplanations.d: Class II tools still need user visual checks and periodic inspection, though testing may be less frequent.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Class II tools lack earth pin; design prevents accessible parts becoming live — still avoid damage and wet misuse. Reinforced insulation can be used as the equivalent of the two layers.
