options.a: Fitted behind a lockable cover to prevent accidental operation
options.b: Set so that releasing or twisting the stop button restarts the machine immediately
options.c: Easily accessible, clearly identifiable, and override start functions until reset
options.d: Used as the means of isolation during maintenance work

distractorExplanations.a: Covers that slow access defeat the purpose of an emergency stop; it must be reachable immediately.
distractorExplanations.b: Resetting an emergency stop must not restart hazardous motion; a separate deliberate start action is required.
distractorExplanations.d: An emergency stop is not an isolator; maintenance requires isolation and lock-off of the energy supply.

options.a: Standard lifts for evacuation, as they are the fastest route down
options.b: Locating mobility-impaired staff on upper floors so they are close to the refuge
options.c: Leaving them at refuge points until the fire service arrives
options.d: Personal emergency evacuation plans (PEEPs) and refuge areas with communication

distractorExplanations.a: Normal lifts can fail or open on the fire floor; designated evacuation lifts are the exception.
distractorExplanations.b: Ground-floor placement simplifies evacuation; PEEPs plan assistance rather than relying on an upstairs location.
distractorExplanations.c: Refuges are temporary; the employer must plan onward evacuation rather than rely on the fire service.

options.a: Blade guard, riving knife, push stick, dust extraction, training, and maintenance
options.b: Blade guard and push stick, with disposable dust masks used instead of extraction
options.c: Riving knife and training, with blade guard removed for narrow cuts
options.d: Noise levels and operator training, with kickback controlled by firm hand pressure

distractorExplanations.b: Wood dust is a carcinogen and sensitiser; LEV at source comes before RPE, and the riving knife is left out.
distractorExplanations.c: The blade guard must stay on for narrow cuts; push sticks are used to keep hands away instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Kickback is controlled by the riving knife and correct feed, not by pushing harder with the hands.

options.a: Allowing production to continue alongside maintenance with temporary barriers
options.b: Scheduling isolation windows, competent persons, and testing before return to service
options.c: Scheduling maintenance by competent staff, with dead testing carried out if time allows
options.d: Resetting tripped RCDs repeatedly until the circuit holds, then logging it

distractorExplanations.a: Running production while maintenance is under way risks unexpected energisation; planned isolation windows are needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Proving dead is essential every time before work, not optional when time permits.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeated tripping indicates a fault that a competent person must investigate, not something to keep resetting.

nebosh-readiness-check-equipment-fire-el.explanation: Planned maintenance embeds isolation, competence, and verification — aligning PUWER and electricity regs. Spare guards should be on hand so equipment is not returned without guarding.

options.a: Identify the hazards associated with the activity or workplace
options.b: Decide who might be harmed and how, including visitors and contractors
options.c: Evaluate the risks and decide on suitable precautions
options.d: Record the significant findings and implement controls

distractorExplanations.b: Deciding who might be harmed is the second step; hazards must be identified before you can say who they affect.
distractorExplanations.c: Evaluating risks comes after hazards and the people at risk are identified; it is the third step.
distractorExplanations.d: Recording significant findings comes after hazards are identified and risks evaluated, near the end of the process.

options.a: Lists every hazard in detail, including trivial ones, for each task
options.b: Identifies significant risks, considers those affected, and outlines adequate controls
options.c: Is signed off by a chartered safety professional and reviewed on a fixed five-year cycle
options.d: Uses a generic template from the group covering the site's routine work

distractorExplanations.a: Suitable and sufficient means proportionate; trivial risks need not be recorded, and excessive detail obscures significant ones.
distractorExplanations.c: Competence matters, but no chartered signature is required, and review is triggered by change rather than a fixed five-year cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Generic templates can overlook site-specific and non-routine tasks; the assessment must reflect the actual activity.

nebosh-readiness-check-gic2-risk-assessm.explanation: Suitable and sufficient means proportionate, task-specific where needed, and actionable for significant risks. It should also be specific enough to the activity being assessed.

options.a: Remove the need for controls on risks that score in the green band
options.b: Calculate the exact probability of an accident occurring for insurance purposes
options.c: Demonstrate legal compliance by itself without further action
options.d: Prioritise controls for higher-rated risks and communicate residual risk

distractorExplanations.a: Low-rated risks still need existing controls maintained; the matrix ranks priority, it does not remove duties.
distractorExplanations.b: Risk matrices give a semi-quantitative ranking for prioritising action, not exact probabilities.
distractorExplanations.c: A score does not equal compliance; controls must still be implemented and maintained.

options.a: Inexperience, maturity, training needs, and prohibited high-risk tasks for young persons
options.b: The same factors as adult workers, with extra supervision for the first week
options.c: Parental consent forms, which transfer legal responsibility for safety to the parents
options.d: Physical strength only, since young persons have the same awareness of risk

distractorExplanations.b: Young persons need a specific assessment of immaturity and inexperience with ongoing supervision, not just one week.
distractorExplanations.c: Parents may be informed of risks, but their consent does not transfer the employer's legal duty of care.
distractorExplanations.d: Young workers typically lack risk awareness and experience; physical strength is one factor among several.

options.a: A fixed period of five years has elapsed since the assessment was first written
options.b: There is reason to suspect it is no longer valid or after significant change
options.c: The regulator requests a copy during a routine inspection visit
options.d: A worker complains, but not after a near miss with no injury

distractorExplanations.a: Review is triggered by change, incidents or doubt about validity, not by waiting for a fixed five-year cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Reviews should be proactive; waiting for a regulator to ask for the document is reactive.
distractorExplanations.d: Near misses are important review triggers because they show controls may have failed even without injury.

nebosh-readiness-check-gic2-risk-assessm.explanation: Review triggers include new processes, equipment, legislation, accidents, and complaints — not arbitrary daily rewrite. Incidents and near misses are also triggers for review.

options.a: Record it only if it has already caused an injury in the past year
options.b: Recommend stopping the whole site's work until the area is cleared
options.c: Record the finding, discuss significance, and recommend corrective actions linked to risk
options.d: Note it as a training issue for the cleaning team and take no further management action

distractorExplanations.a: Inspections are proactive; hazards are recorded on their potential to cause harm, not on injury history.
distractorExplanations.b: Recommendations must be proportionate; poor housekeeping usually needs prompt clean-up and storage fixes, not a site-wide stop.
distractorExplanations.d: Blaming the cleaners ignores management causes such as storage and schedules; recommendations should address root causes.

options.a: List the hazards in the workplace that could cause harm to people
options.b: Decide which workers, contractors and visitors might be harmed and how they are exposed
options.c: Record the significant findings and share them with affected workers
options.d: Estimate likelihood and severity of harm from each hazard considering existing controls

distractorExplanations.a: Listing hazards is the first step; evaluation then estimates the level of risk each one poses.
distractorExplanations.b: Identifying who may be harmed is the second step; the evaluation step judges likelihood and severity.
distractorExplanations.c: Recording findings happens after evaluation, once the significant risks and controls are known.

options.a: Replacing a toxic solvent with a less harmful water-based alternative
options.b: Enclosing the solvent process and fitting local exhaust ventilation
options.c: Issuing chemical-resistant gloves while the same solvent stays in use
options.d: Reducing the time each worker spends using the solvent each day

distractorExplanations.b: Enclosure and LEV are engineering controls; the hazardous solvent itself is still in use.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE is the lowest level of the hierarchy and does not change the hazard of the solvent.
distractorExplanations.d: Limiting exposure time is an administrative control, not substitution of the substance.

options.a: Completed once at notification and kept on file for the pregnancy
options.b: Completed with medical input as needed and reviewed as pregnancy progresses
options.c: Left to the worker's GP, who decides what tasks she may continue
options.d: Limited to manual handling, as chemical risks are already covered by COSHH assessments

distractorExplanations.a: Risks change as pregnancy progresses, so the assessment must be reviewed, not done once and filed.
distractorExplanations.c: Medical advice informs the assessment, but the duty to assess and adjust work stays with the employer.
distractorExplanations.d: Pregnancy assessments must consider chemical, biological, physical and stress risks to mother and unborn child.

nebosh-readiness-check-gic2-risk-assessm.explanation: Pregnancy assessments address changing capacity and legal protections; dialogue and review are required. It should cover manual handling, chemicals, and stress.

options.a: The consequence of the event would be a fatality or major injury
options.b: The task is rarely done but involves a highly toxic substance
options.c: The hazardous event occurs frequently or controls are consistently bypassed
options.d: Workers are trained, closely supervised, and controls are inspected every week

distractorExplanations.a: That raises severity, not likelihood; the two axes of the matrix are scored separately.
distractorExplanations.b: Toxicity affects severity, while doing the task rarely lowers likelihood.
distractorExplanations.d: Training, supervision and regular inspection reduce likelihood rather than increase it.

options.a: Documenting every hazard identified, including trivial ones
options.b: Recording the assessor's name and date, with findings kept verbally
options.c: Keeping findings with management and away from the workers who carry out the task
options.d: Documenting hazards, who is at risk, controls, and priorities for significant risks

distractorExplanations.a: Significant findings are what must be recorded; listing trivial hazards obscures priorities.
distractorExplanations.b: Findings must be written down and communicated, not kept verbally by the assessor.
distractorExplanations.c: Findings must be communicated to those affected so they understand and follow the controls.

options.a: Enclosing the machine or installing silencers to reduce emitted noise
options.b: Issuing ear defenders with an attenuation rating matched to the measured noise level
options.c: Rotating workers so each spends less time near the machine
options.d: Posting hearing protection zone signs at the machine area

distractorExplanations.b: Hearing protection is PPE, the last resort in the hierarchy, not an engineering control.
distractorExplanations.c: Job rotation is an administrative control that limits exposure time without reducing the noise.
distractorExplanations.d: Signs are administrative information, not engineering reduction of the noise source.

options.a: Ask closed yes/no questions so the answers are quick to record
options.b: Ask open questions, listen without blame, and clarify task, hazards, and controls
options.c: Interview the worker with their manager present to ensure accuracy
options.d: Focus on establishing what the worker did wrong so corrective training can follow

distractorExplanations.a: Closed questions limit information; open questions reveal what actually happened and why.
distractorExplanations.c: A manager's presence can inhibit honest answers; interview privately or with a representative if requested.
distractorExplanations.d: A blame focus discourages reporting and ignores the underlying causes of the near miss.

options.a: Medium because a harness is available on site if needed
options.b: Low because falls from 6 m rarely happen on this site
options.c: High because potential outcome includes serious injury or fatality
options.d: Medium because the worker has many years of experience working at height

distractorExplanations.a: A harness being available does not reduce severity when the fall is unprotected.
distractorExplanations.b: Rarity affects likelihood, not severity; the consequence of a 6 m fall is still serious.
distractorExplanations.d: Experience may affect likelihood, but the consequence of a 6 m fall remains severe.

options.a: Fitting interlocked guards to the machinery used in the hazardous work area
options.b: Replacing a solvent-based cleaner with a water-based one
options.c: Issuing gloves, goggles, and hearing protection to workers
options.d: Job rotation, permit-to-work, and supervised access to hazardous area

distractorExplanations.a: Interlocked guards are engineering controls, higher in the hierarchy than administrative controls.
distractorExplanations.b: That is substitution, which changes the hazard itself rather than the procedures for working with it.
distractorExplanations.c: Those are PPE, the last level of the hierarchy, below administrative controls.

options.a: Reviewed to reflect reduced inhalation risk and verify maintenance arrangements
options.b: Left unchanged, as LEV was already listed as a planned control
options.c: Archived and replaced by the LEV commissioning report
options.d: Reviewed after the first annual LEV thorough examination has been completed

distractorExplanations.b: Introducing a new control is a change that requires review to verify it actually works.
distractorExplanations.c: Commissioning reports verify LEV performance but do not assess the whole welding task.
distractorExplanations.d: Review should happen when the change is made, not be delayed until the first examination.

nebosh-readiness-check-gic2-risk-assessm.explanation: Control changes trigger assessment review to ensure risks are now adequately controlled. Thorough examination arrangements for the new LEV should also be confirmed.

options.a: Desk-based display screen work assessed using individual DSE workstation checklists
options.b: Warehouse forklift operations added at the same site without specific assessment
options.c: Office cleaning tasks using low-hazard domestic products
options.d: Visitors attending meetings in the office conference room

distractorExplanations.a: DSE work fits within an office assessment when individual workstations are assessed.
distractorExplanations.c: Low-hazard cleaning can be covered generically once it has been assessed.
distractorExplanations.d: Visitors in office areas are covered by the generic office assessment.

options.a: The health and safety manager working alone, to keep the assessment consistent
options.b: Senior management and the insurer, who approve the controls
options.c: Workers doing the task, supervision, and health and safety expertise as needed
options.d: An external consultant, so that workers are not distracted

distractorExplanations.a: Excluding workers loses practical task knowledge, and workers must be consulted on risks affecting them.
distractorExplanations.b: Insurers and senior managers lack task knowledge; those doing the work should be involved.
distractorExplanations.d: Consultants can advise, but workers must be consulted about hazards in their own work.

options.a: The risk level before any controls have been put in place
options.b: The proportion of the risk that is transferred to the insurer by the policy
options.c: The risk that remains only if PPE is not worn by workers
options.d: The remaining risk level assuming controls are implemented and effective

distractorExplanations.a: That describes inherent or initial risk, the opposite of residual risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Insurance transfers financial loss, not the risk of harm to people.
distractorExplanations.c: Residual risk applies after controls are in place, not to a scenario where PPE is not worn.

options.a: Obstructions, door function, signage, lighting, and final exit security
options.b: Fire extinguisher service labels and the fault display on the fire alarm panel
options.c: Floor finishes and decoration standards along the corridor
options.d: Number of occupants who used the route in the last drill

distractorExplanations.b: Extinguishers and panels are fire equipment checks; the route check is about clearance, doors, signs and lighting.
distractorExplanations.c: Decoration does not affect escape; the inspection checks obstructions, doors and signage.
distractorExplanations.d: Drill attendance is a records issue; the physical inspection checks the condition of the route.

options.a: A cost-saving measure to reduce insurance premiums for younger staff
options.b: Legal and risk-based recognition of vulnerability and prohibited hazardous activities
options.c: A requirement that applies to apprentices only, not to other young workers on site
options.d: A preference to keep young persons in office roles until 21

distractorExplanations.a: Restrictions are based on risk and legal duties, not on insurance cost.
distractorExplanations.c: Restrictions apply to every young person under 18, not just apprentices.
distractorExplanations.d: Young persons are those under 18, and restrictions target specific hazardous work, not every practical role.

options.a: Filing the assessment with HR, with workers informed if they ask
options.b: Recording findings, with implementation of controls left to each supervisor's judgement
options.c: Communicating controls, training, and putting identified measures into practice
options.d: Sending the document to the regulator for approval before use

distractorExplanations.a: Findings must be proactively communicated to affected workers, not shared only on request.
distractorExplanations.b: Identified controls must be implemented and monitored by management, not left optional.
distractorExplanations.d: Risk assessments do not need regulator approval; the employer must implement them.

options.a: Medium risk to be addressed at the next annual review
options.b: Low risk where existing controls are adequate and recorded
options.c: Tolerable risk that needs routine monitoring but no additional controls or redesign
options.d: High priority risk requiring urgent additional controls or task redesign

distractorExplanations.a: A score of 20 out of 25 is in the high band, not medium; it needs urgent action.
distractorExplanations.b: A score of 20 sits near the top of a 5x5 matrix (maximum 25); it is not a low risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Tolerable bands are usually low-to-medium scores; a score of 20 requires action.

options.a: Conditions change rapidly on site and the worker must reassess before proceeding
options.b: A written assessment is not required because the task has been judged low risk
options.c: Routine tasks are repeated in the same conditions every day
options.d: Managers want to avoid writing assessments for new tasks

distractorExplanations.b: Dynamic assessment supplements written assessments; it does not replace them.
distractorExplanations.c: Unchanging routine tasks are covered by the existing written assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: New tasks need a written assessment; dynamic assessment handles changes on the spot.

options.a: Issuing gloves and goggles first, then reviewing other controls at a later date
options.b: Choosing gloves and goggles only after considering substitution and enclosure
options.c: Using gloves instead of guarding because the press is rarely used
options.d: Choosing PPE because it is cheaper than engineering controls

distractorExplanations.a: Issuing PPE first reverses the hierarchy; higher controls must be considered before PPE.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE cannot replace machine guarding, and infrequent use does not change the hierarchy.
distractorExplanations.d: Cost alone does not justify skipping higher controls; PPE is used when residual risk remains.

nebosh-readiness-check-gic2-risk-assessm.explanation: Hierarchy requires higher controls first; PPE supplements when residual risk remains. Here this applies to a corrosive splash task.

options.a: A standard pre-placement medical with exclusion if any condition is found
options.b: The same assessment as other staff, since disclosure creates no new duties
options.c: Individual assessment of reasonable adjustments without blanket exclusion from role
options.d: Restriction to office duties until a specialist occupational health report is received

distractorExplanations.a: Blanket exclusion based on any condition is discriminatory; capability must be assessed individually.
distractorExplanations.b: Disclosure triggers a duty to consider reasonable adjustments and individual risk factors.
distractorExplanations.d: Automatic restriction is a blanket approach; adjustments should follow an individual assessment.

options.a: List every hazard observed in equal detail without ranking, so management can choose which ones to address first
options.b: Focus on the legal penalties faced, omitting the cost, timescale and practicality of each recommended control
options.c: Rely on the checklist score alone, since interviews with workers introduce opinion rather than objective evidence
options.d: Present findings clearly, prioritise recommendations, and use evidence from inspection and interviews

distractorExplanations.a: Unranked lists fail GIC2: recommendations must be prioritised by risk, not left for management to sort out.
distractorExplanations.b: Legal argument alone is incomplete; GIC2 recommendations need realistic cost, timescale and practicality.
distractorExplanations.c: Worker interviews are legitimate evidence in GIC2; excluding them loses information on how work is really done.

options.a: May still require control if cumulative exposure or interaction creates significant combined risk
options.b: Can be screened out as trivial, because each risk is assessed separately against its own severity rating
options.c: Should be recorded once under the highest single risk, since lower risks are absorbed by that control
options.d: Needs action only when one of the individual risks reaches medium on the matrix, not before

distractorExplanations.b: Ignores the cumulative effect; several individually low risks at one workstation can combine into a significant risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Assumes controlling the worst risk covers the others; different hazards (posture, noise, lighting) need their own controls.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies a single-risk threshold; the combined exposure can be significant even when no single score reaches medium.

options.a: Direct employees on the payroll, since contractors and agency staff are covered by their own employers' assessments
options.b: Employees, contractors, visitors, public, and vulnerable groups such as young or disabled workers
options.c: Workers who perform the task, plus supervisors, as visitors and the public are covered by premises insurance
options.d: Groups of workers by job title, without singling out young, pregnant or disabled workers to avoid discrimination

distractorExplanations.a: Host employers must consider contractors and agency workers affected by their activities; duties are shared, not transferred.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses insurance with risk assessment; visitors and members of the public affected by work activities must be identified.
distractorExplanations.d: Identifying vulnerable groups is required for suitable controls; assessing their specific risks is not discrimination.

options.a: The maintenance task method alone, since production hazards are covered by the line's own assessment
options.b: Production output targets and downtime cost, with isolation planned once access becomes difficult
options.c: Simultaneous operations (SIMOPS), isolation, communication, and fire/explosion interfaces
options.d: Contractor competence checks and PPE issue, with permits reserved for work after production stops

distractorExplanations.a: Separate assessments miss the interface; maintenance during production creates combined hazards that must be assessed together.
distractorExplanations.b: Isolation must be planned and verified before work begins; deferring it until access is difficult exposes maintainers to live plant.
distractorExplanations.d: Permits are most needed when maintenance overlaps live production; reserving them for shutdown work ignores the higher-risk case.

options.a: The level the organisation's risk matrix labels tolerable, without considering further practicable controls
options.b: Zero where technically possible, with cost considered only once every engineering option is exhausted
options.c: The level achieved by industry peers, so controls matching common sector practice are sufficient
options.d: As low as reasonably practicable — balancing risk, cost, and benefit of further controls

distractorExplanations.a: A matrix 'tolerable' band is not ALARP; further controls must still be adopted unless their cost is grossly disproportionate.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes an absolute 'so far as is possible' duty; ALARP weighs cost against risk rather than demanding every technical option.
distractorExplanations.c: Industry practice is a benchmark, not a ceiling; ALARP may require more than peers do if the risk justifies it.

options.a: Risk level, feasibility, and legal compliance gaps observed during inspection
options.b: Cost of each action, starting with the cheapest so that quick wins are reported first
options.c: The order hazards were found on the walk-round, so the report follows the inspection route
options.d: Management's stated preferences, so the actions most likely to be approved come first

distractorExplanations.b: Cost alone ignores risk; GIC2 priorities should start with the highest risks and legal breaches, not the cheapest fixes.
distractorExplanations.c: Route order is a presentation convenience; recommendations must be ranked by risk level and urgency.
distractorExplanations.d: Acceptability to management is not a risk criterion; serious risks must be prioritised even if unwelcome.

options.a: Treat the agency as holding the health and safety duties, as it is the worker's legal employer
options.b: Cooperate to ensure induction, risk assessment coverage, and clear safety responsibilities
options.c: Leave site induction to the agency, which briefs workers on general hazards before placement
options.d: Rely on the host's assessment for permanent staff, as temporary workers face identical risks

distractorExplanations.a: The host controls the workplace and the work, so it keeps duties for site hazards; the agency cannot discharge them alone.
distractorExplanations.c: The agency cannot know site-specific hazards; the host must provide site induction and task-specific information.
distractorExplanations.d: Temporary workers may lack experience and familiarity with the site; the assessment must consider their specific needs.

options.a: Technical feasibility alone, so any control that can be engineered must be fitted at any cost
options.b: The employer's current budget, so controls are deferred when the year's safety allocation is spent
options.c: Gravity and likelihood of harm versus sacrifice (cost, time, difficulty) in money terms
options.d: Likelihood of harm alone, so rare events need no further control however severe the outcome

distractorExplanations.a: That is the stricter 'so far as is possible' standard; reasonably practicable weighs cost and effort against the risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Ability to pay is not the test; the sacrifice is judged against the risk, not against the employer's available budget.
distractorExplanations.d: Ignores severity; reasonably practicable weighs both gravity and likelihood of harm against cost, time and difficulty.

options.a: Be limited to incidents that caused injury, as near misses lack severity data
options.b: Wait for the next scheduled annual review before any assessment change is made
options.c: Add retraining for the worker involved, leaving the written assessment unchanged
options.d: Update controls when investigation shows failed or missing controls

distractorExplanations.a: Near misses reveal the same control failures without the injury; excluding them throws away free learning.
distractorExplanations.b: A near miss showing failed controls is a trigger for prompt review, not something to hold until the annual cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the near miss as individual error; if controls failed, the assessment and the controls themselves need updating.

options.a: Segregate or guard the equipment, restrict access, and review PUWER assessment for location
options.b: Fit a warning sign and floor markings around the drill, and brief walkway users at the next toolbox talk
options.c: Issue safety glasses and gloves to people using the walkway until the drill can be relocated
options.d: Record the hazard for the report and recommend guarding within the next quarterly maintenance cycle

distractorExplanations.b: Signs and briefings are lower-order controls; an unguarded drill beside a busy walkway needs guarding or segregation first.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE is the last resort and gloves near rotating drills add an entanglement risk; guarding and segregation come first.
distractorExplanations.d: An unguarded drill beside a busy walkway is an immediate danger; deferring action to a quarterly cycle is not acceptable.

options.a: Holding a recognised safety qualification, which on its own demonstrates competence for any workplace
options.b: Understanding hazards, legal duties, control options, and ability to involve workers
options.c: Detailed knowledge of the process, so assessments are best done alone by the most senior engineer
options.d: Familiarity with the risk matrix and scoring software, as numerical ratings drive every decision

distractorExplanations.a: A qualification alone is not competence; experience, site knowledge and the ability to apply it matter too.
distractorExplanations.c: Process knowledge helps, but excluding workers loses practical hazard insight; competence includes involving them.
distractorExplanations.d: Scoring tools are aids; competence rests on understanding hazards and control options, not on operating a matrix.

options.a: The initial risk assessment, which confirms effectiveness when the controls are first installed
options.b: The annual management review, where effectiveness is judged from the year's lost-time injury rate
options.c: Ongoing health and safety management — inspections, audits, exposure monitoring, and incident review
options.d: The control supplier, whose commissioning certificate confirms performance for the whole of the equipment's life

distractorExplanations.a: A one-off check at installation cannot show controls stay effective; degradation and bypassing need ongoing monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Relies on a single lagging indicator once a year; control effectiveness needs active monitoring throughout the year.
distractorExplanations.d: Commissioning shows initial performance; the employer must monitor controls in use, e.g. periodic LEV examination.

options.a: Adjustable bench height combined with planned rotation between tasks
options.b: Lighter cartons with hand-holds and lifting aids for the heavier items
options.c: Enforced micro-breaks with a slower line speed during peak periods
options.d: Higher pace, force, awkward postures, and lack of rotation or breaks

distractorExplanations.a: Adjustable benches and rotation reduce ergonomic risk; they are controls, not factors that increase severity.
distractorExplanations.b: Lighter loads with good grips and lifting aids lower force demands, so they reduce rather than increase severity.
distractorExplanations.c: Micro-breaks and a slower pace give recovery time; these reduce ergonomic risk rather than increase it.

options.a: Still consider robust controls because credible worst case is intolerable
options.b: Accept the risk, since low likelihood offsets high severity on a 5x5 matrix
options.c: Rely on emergency response plans instead of preventive controls, as the event is rare
options.d: Transfer the risk through insurance, which covers low-probability high-loss events

distractorExplanations.b: Matrix scoring can hide catastrophic outcomes; an intolerable credible worst case needs robust controls whatever the score.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency plans mitigate after the event; prevention must still be pursued for a credible catastrophic scenario.
distractorExplanations.d: Insurance moves financial loss, not the risk of harm; the legal duty to control the hazard stays with the employer.

options.a: Present every inspection finding in detail so managers can see the full extent of the work
options.b: Summarise key risks, legal implications, and prioritized actions with timescales
options.c: Focus on the moral case for change, leaving legal and financial arguments to the written report
options.d: Lead with the cost of each control, so managers can approve actions within the current budget

distractorExplanations.a: Exhaustive detail buries priorities; a management presentation should summarise key risks and ranked actions.
distractorExplanations.c: Managers need the moral, legal and financial case together; dropping legal implications weakens the argument.
distractorExplanations.d: Starting with cost frames safety as budget-driven; priorities should follow risk level and legal duty.

options.a: They create a legal record that shifts liability for any injury onto the visitor
options.b: They are only valid if countersigned by a director rather than a host or receptionist
options.c: They do not communicate site-specific hazards and controls at time of visit
options.d: They should be replaced by a written risk assessment completed by each visitor

distractorExplanations.a: Signatures cannot transfer the occupier's duty of care; the real weakness is the lack of hazard communication.
distractorExplanations.b: Countersignature level is not the issue; no signature fixes the absence of a site-specific briefing.
distractorExplanations.d: Visitors are not expected to assess the site; the host should brief them on relevant hazards and controls.

options.a: Recording every hazard identified, including trivial ones, so the file is complete for inspectors
options.b: Logging the residual risk scores in a central register kept confidential to the safety team
options.c: Reviewing the assessment and updating it when work changes or after an incident occurs
options.d: Writing down the assessment results for significant risks and sharing with workforce

distractorExplanations.a: Step 4 focuses on significant findings; recording trivial hazards dilutes the assessment.
distractorExplanations.b: Findings must be shared with the workers affected; keeping them confidential defeats the purpose of recording.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes Step 5 (review and update), not Step 4 (record significant findings and share them).

options.a: DSE setup, stress/isolation, electrical safety, trips, and emergency arrangements
options.b: DSE setup and posture, with electrical and trip hazards left to the homeowner's insurance
options.c: Workstation ergonomics alone, as psychosocial risks are assessed separately for office staff
options.d: A one-off self-assessment checklist at hire, with no review needed when duties change

distractorExplanations.b: Employer duties extend to work equipment and work activities at home; electrical and trip risks still need assessing.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolation and stress are key homeworking risks; a homeworker assessment should include them, not defer to office studies.
distractorExplanations.d: Homeworker assessments need review when tasks, equipment or health change; a one-off check at hire is insufficient.

options.a: Replacing written descriptions, as images make risk ratings unnecessary
options.b: Providing objective evidence of hazards observed for the report
options.c: Identifying the workers at fault so disciplinary action can follow
options.d: Proving compliance, since a clear photo shows a hazard is controlled

distractorExplanations.a: Photos support but cannot replace written description and risk evaluation of each hazard.
distractorExplanations.c: Inspection photos record conditions, not blame; using them to target individuals undermines reporting culture.
distractorExplanations.d: A snapshot shows one moment; it cannot prove ongoing control or legal compliance on its own.

options.a: Simple, minimal, agreed, reviewed, and tracked by the safety department
options.b: Strategic, monitored, audited, reported, and targeted at lagging indicators
options.c: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound where possible
options.d: Short, mandatory, approved, reasonable, and tied to the next audit date

distractorExplanations.a: Wrong expansion of SMART; it stands for specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
distractorExplanations.b: Misexpands SMART with audit vocabulary; SMART recommendations are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes in approval and audit terms; SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

options.a: Unchanged residual risk, as the hazard itself has not been removed
options.b: Higher initial risk score, since new equipment adds unfamiliar hazards
options.c: Lower inherent risk score, as engineering controls remove the hazard
options.d: Lower residual risk score reflecting improved hierarchy position

distractorExplanations.a: Engineering controls reduce likelihood or exposure, so residual risk falls even though the hazard remains.
distractorExplanations.b: The initial (inherent) rating is not changed by controls; the upgrade should lower the residual risk score.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses inherent and residual risk; engineering reduces residual risk, it does not change the uncontrolled rating.

options.a: Honesty, confidentiality where appropriate, and professional behaviour without falsifying findings
options.b: Reporting only findings that management has agreed in advance, to keep the inspection constructive
options.c: Naming individual workers seen breaking rules so the report has clear accountability for each breach
options.d: Softening serious findings into general observations to protect the working relationship with the host

distractorExplanations.b: Pre-agreeing findings compromises honesty; the inspector must report what was actually observed.
distractorExplanations.c: Naming individuals breaches confidentiality and shifts focus to blame; reports should address system failures.
distractorExplanations.d: Downgrading serious findings is a form of falsification; GIC2 ethics require accurate reporting.

options.a: Preparing a site emergency plan once a year, separate from task risk assessments to keep both concise
options.b: Identifying scenarios requiring evacuation, rescue, or medical response and linking to procedures
options.c: Limiting emergency planning to fire, as other scenarios are covered by first-aid arrangements
options.d: Leaving rescue to public emergency services, so assessments need not consider on-site rescue

distractorExplanations.a: Separating the plans misses task-specific scenarios such as confined-space rescue that assessments should feed into.
distractorExplanations.c: Chemical release, collapse, rescue at height and medical events need planned responses beyond first aid.
distractorExplanations.d: Public services may not arrive in time for confined-space or height rescue; on-site rescue plans are required.

options.a: Provide a mechanical lift or raise the load source to waist height to reduce bending and manual exertion
options.b: Issue a back support belt and train the worker in kinetic lifting technique for lifting the floor-level sacks
options.c: Introduce job rotation so each operative lifts the sacks for no more than two hours per shift
options.d: Refer the worker to occupational health and restrict lifting until the back pain has resolved

distractorExplanations.b: Belts and technique training are lower-order controls (PPE/administrative); the task design itself stays unchanged.
distractorExplanations.c: Rotation spreads exposure but leaves floor-level lifting in place; elimination or engineering controls come first.
distractorExplanations.d: Health referral helps the individual but does not control the task risk for every operative lifting the sacks.

options.a: Moderate load, waist-height pick-up, two-person lift, and scheduled rest breaks
options.b: Heavy load, awkward posture, limited grip, and insufficient recovery time between lifts
options.c: Light load lifted at shoulder height occasionally, with handles and good footing
options.d: Bulky but light load carried close to the body over a short level distance

distractorExplanations.a: These are lower-risk conditions under TILE; waist height, team lifting and rest breaks reduce injury risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Occasional light lifts with handles are low risk; heavy load plus poor posture and no recovery is far worse.
distractorExplanations.d: Light loads held close over short level distances give low spinal loading compared with heavy, awkward repeated lifts.

options.a: Supply a laptop stand for sofa use and remind the worker to take short breaks every two hours
options.b: Arrange an eyesight test and provide corrective glasses for screen work at the employer's cost, keeping the sofa setup
options.c: Provide a suitable DSE workstation with adjustable chair, external keyboard/mouse, and screen at eye level
options.d: Refer the worker for physiotherapy and keep the current sofa setup while treatment continues

distractorExplanations.a: A stand on a sofa still leaves poor seated posture and no keyboard separation; a proper DSE workstation is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Eye tests address visual strain, not the neck and wrist pain caused by sofa posture and laptop keyboard use.
distractorExplanations.d: Treatment addresses symptoms but leaves the cause; the workstation itself must be corrected first.

options.a: A single short exposure to impulse noise of around 100 dB(A) during a weekly fire alarm test
options.b: Long hours at around 70 dB(A) in an open-plan office with continuous background conversation
options.c: Occasional exposure above action levels with correctly fitted, suitable hearing protection worn throughout
options.d: Regular exposure above action levels without adequate hearing protection or engineering controls

distractorExplanations.a: Isolated brief exposures at that level are unlikely to cause NIHL; the risk builds from regular cumulative exposure.
distractorExplanations.b: 70 dB(A) is below the action values; NIHL is linked to regular exposure above 80-85 dB(A).
distractorExplanations.c: Suitable, correctly worn protection reduces exposure at the ear; regular unprotected exposure is the main risk pattern.

options.a: Hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS) from prolonged use of vibrating tools
options.b: Whole-body vibration transmitted through the feet from standing on the tool
options.c: Raynaud's disease caused by cold weather alone, unrelated to the work tasks
options.d: Carpal tunnel syndrome caused mainly by repetitive gripping of the handles

distractorExplanations.b: WBV affects the back via the seat or feet; finger blanching and tingling are hand-arm vibration symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: Cold triggers attacks, but finger blanching in a jackhammer user points to vibration white finger (HAVS).
distractorExplanations.d: Carpal tunnel causes tingling but not cold-triggered blanching; the vascular signs indicate HAVS.

options.a: Salt tablets and energy drinks at the gate, with breaks taken at the end of each shift
options.b: Shelter, potable drinking water, toilet facilities, and rest breaks to manage heat stress
options.c: Cooling vests for every worker, which remove the need for shaded rest areas and breaks
options.d: Toilet and washing facilities at the nearest town, with water bottles supplied on request

distractorExplanations.a: Salt tablets and end-of-shift breaks do not manage heat stress; shaded rest and potable water through the day do.
distractorExplanations.c: Cooling PPE supplements but cannot replace shade, water and rest breaks on a hot remote site.
distractorExplanations.d: Welfare facilities must be accessible on site; facilities in town and water on request are inadequate.

options.a: Offer an employee assistance programme and stress-management training for staff, while leaving targets and workload unchanged
options.b: Refer absent staff to occupational health and require fitness certificates before return to work
options.c: Review workload, targets, support resources, and consultation with workers to identify psychosocial risk factors
options.d: Introduce a resilience workshop and absence management policy with triggers for formal review

distractorExplanations.a: EAPs and training are individual-level support; the organisational causes such as workload and targets remain.
distractorExplanations.b: OH referral manages individual cases but does not identify or control the team-wide psychosocial causes.
distractorExplanations.d: Absence triggers and resilience training focus on the worker, not on the work design driving stress.

options.a: Confirm the screen meets electrical safety standards and record the date of its last portable appliance test on file
options.b: Determine whether the user is entitled to employer-funded eye tests and record the outcome for payroll
options.c: Measure office temperature, humidity and lighting levels to confirm compliance with building regulations
options.d: Identify ergonomic risks from screen work and implement adjustments to reduce musculoskeletal and visual strain

distractorExplanations.a: PAT testing addresses electrical safety, not the ergonomic and visual risks a DSE assessment targets.
distractorExplanations.b: Eye tests follow from DSE duties but are not the assessment's primary purpose of identifying workstation risks.
distractorExplanations.c: Environmental checks are part of the picture, but a DSE assessment targets the user's workstation and posture.

options.a: Hearing protection zone, training, and health surveillance where required, plus programme to reduce exposure
options.b: Hearing protection made available on request and information to workers, with no zone or noise programme
options.c: Annual audiometry for exposed workers as the main action, with hearing protection left to each worker's own choice
options.d: Noise reduction programme only, with hearing protection deferred until engineering options are exhausted

distractorExplanations.b: That is the lower action value response; at 90 dB(A) protection must be worn in marked zones with a reduction programme.
distractorExplanations.c: At 90 dB(A) hearing protection is mandatory in marked zones; audiometry monitors damage without preventing it.
distractorExplanations.d: Engineering comes first, but above the upper action value protection must be worn while the programme proceeds.

options.a: Hold the load at arm's length to keep it clear of the body, bend at the waist and lift smoothly in one movement
options.b: Keep the load close to the body, use leg muscles, avoid twisting, and team-lift if the load is unstable or too heavy
options.c: Keep the back straight and legs locked, turning the feet rather than twisting, and lift with a fast jerk to save time
options.d: Squat fully with the load in front, twist to the destination at waist height, and team-lift only loads over 50 kg

distractorExplanations.a: Holding the load away from the body multiplies spinal loading; loads should be held close with the knees bent.
distractorExplanations.c: Locked legs and jerky lifts increase spinal stress; good technique uses the legs and smooth, controlled movement.
distractorExplanations.d: Twisting under load is a major injury factor, and 50 kg is far above the point where team lifting or aids are needed.

options.a: It reduces exposure duration so effectively that workstation redesign becomes unnecessary for most tasks
options.b: It increases training costs, which is the main reason ergonomists advise against rotation in assembly
options.c: It may spread exposure to different MSD risks without reducing total ergonomic hazard in the job design
options.d: It only works when workers rotate between tasks using the same muscle groups for consistency

distractorExplanations.a: Rotation shortens individual exposure but leaves the hazard in the task; redesign remains the higher-order control.
distractorExplanations.b: Training cost is a practical issue, not the main limitation; the key weakness is that the hazards remain in the job.
distractorExplanations.d: Reversed logic; rotation must move workers to tasks using different muscle groups so that tissues can recover.

options.a: Operating hand-held breakers and grinders on concrete floors for several hours during each shift
options.b: Using a hand-guided floor polisher on smooth surfaces during office cleaning work
options.c: Driving a passenger car on smooth motorways for short daily commutes to site
options.d: Driving off-road plant such as dumpers and forklifts on uneven ground for extended periods

distractorExplanations.a: Breakers and grinders cause hand-arm vibration; WBV comes through the seat or feet from mobile plant.
distractorExplanations.b: Hand-guided machines transmit vibration mainly to the hands and arms, not through the whole body.
distractorExplanations.c: Smooth-road car driving gives low WBV; the risk is with off-road plant on rough ground for long periods.

options.a: Review shift length, rest between shifts, workload, and fatigue policy with worker involvement
options.b: Provide caffeine and bright lighting on night shifts, keeping shift patterns as currently rostered
options.c: Move the nurse to day shifts permanently while keeping the current night roster for colleagues
options.d: Add a second checker for medication errors on nights, leaving shift length and rest unchanged

distractorExplanations.b: Caffeine and lighting mask the symptoms but leave the roster that causes fatigue unchanged.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving one worker helps the individual but leaves the fatigue risk in the roster for everyone else.
distractorExplanations.d: Double-checking catches errors but does not address the fatigue that causes them in the first place.

options.a: Temporary tingling that resolves within minutes of stopping the tool at end of shift
options.b: Persistent numbness, loss of grip strength, and finger blanching after tool use
options.c: Mild aching in the forearm after a long shift that settles fully overnight with rest
options.d: Reddened palms and sweaty hands after using the tool with heavy gloves in warm weather

distractorExplanations.a: Brief tingling that settles quickly is common; persistent numbness and blanching indicate HAVS needing referral.
distractorExplanations.c: Aching that resolves overnight is non-specific fatigue; vascular and neurological signs warrant urgent referral.
distractorExplanations.d: Redness and sweating from gloves are not HAVS signs; finger blanching and loss of sensation are.

options.a: Wrist splints worn during keying, plus higher screens placed above eye level for posture
options.b: Faster keyboards with shortcut training, so staff complete their keying targets sooner
options.c: Adjustable chairs, neutral wrist posture, ergonomic keyboards or rests, and micro-breaks
options.d: Fixed-height desks with hard wrist edges, and breaks taken together at lunch only

distractorExplanations.a: Splints are PPE-level, and screens above eye level cause neck extension; workstation design comes first.
distractorExplanations.b: Shortcuts may cut keystrokes, but faster targets increase repetition; neutral posture and breaks address the pain.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixed heights and contact stress worsen forearm pain; adjustability and regular micro-breaks are needed.

options.a: Take no action until daily exposure exceeds the upper exposure action value of 85 dB(A)
options.b: Make protection compulsory in a marked zone and stop work until exposure is below 80 dB(A)
options.c: Rely on annual audiometry to detect hearing change before deciding whether controls are needed
options.d: Provide suitable hearing protection, training in use, and plan noise reduction measures

distractorExplanations.a: Duties start at the lower action value (80 dB(A)); information, training and available protection are required.
distractorExplanations.b: Stopping work is not required at this level; compulsory zones apply above the upper action value of 85 dB(A).
distractorExplanations.c: Audiometry monitors for damage; it is not a substitute for protection and noise reduction at this exposure.

options.a: Review of load limits, posture, rest, medical advice, and task modification as pregnancy progresses
options.b: A single assessment when pregnancy is notified, kept unchanged until the worker starts maternity leave
options.c: Transfer the worker to non-lifting duties without discussing alternatives or obtaining medical advice
options.d: Use of the standard guideline lifting weights, as pregnancy does not alter manual handling capability

distractorExplanations.b: Risks change as pregnancy progresses; the assessment must be reviewed, not fixed at the point of notification.
distractorExplanations.c: Changes should follow assessment and medical advice with the worker involved, not be imposed unilaterally.
distractorExplanations.d: Pregnancy affects posture, ligaments and balance; standard guideline weights may need lowering as it progresses.

options.a: Raising overall lux levels as high as possible and positioning screens facing windows
options.b: Balancing ambient and task lighting, reducing glare, and allowing DSE breaks
options.c: Installing blue-light filters on screens while keeping existing lighting unchanged
options.d: Dimming ambient lighting to the minimum so the screen is the main light source

distractorExplanations.a: Excess light and screens facing windows cause glare; balanced lighting and glare control relieve eye strain.
distractorExplanations.c: Filters do not fix poor ambient lighting or glare, which are the main causes of eye strain here.
distractorExplanations.d: Very dim surroundings increase contrast and eye strain; ambient and task lighting should be balanced.

options.a: One worker reporting low mood after a bereavement, with sickness absence over the last month
options.b: Site-wide rise in short absences during winter months, matching the seasonal flu pattern locally
options.c: Multiple workers in the same team reporting high demand, low control, and bullying with rising absence
options.d: A worker requesting flexible hours for childcare, with performance and attendance unchanged

distractorExplanations.a: A single case with a personal trigger points to non-work causes; team-wide patterns indicate work-related stress.
distractorExplanations.b: Seasonal illness explains winter absence; stress shows as clustered demand, control and relationship problems.
distractorExplanations.d: Flexibility requests for caring duties are not stress indicators where performance and attendance are stable.

options.a: Show a recognised manual handling video and test understanding afterwards with a short online quiz
options.b: Teach the straight-back lifting technique using a standard training box in a classroom
options.c: Deliver detailed spinal anatomy lectures so workers understand injury mechanisms fully
options.d: Combine theory on TILE with practical demonstration using actual workplace loads and tasks

distractorExplanations.a: Generic video and quizzes do not build practical skill with the real loads and layouts workers handle.
distractorExplanations.b: Classroom box lifts do not reflect real loads, postures or environments; training should use the actual tasks.
distractorExplanations.c: Anatomy theory without practice on real tasks does not change handling behaviour at the workstation.

options.a: Providing hygienic food preparation areas, seating, hydration, and facilities to eat away from hazardous zones
options.b: Offering subsidised healthy meals and nutrition advice, with eating permitted at workstations to save break time
options.c: Providing vending machines and seating next to the production line so workers stay near their machines
options.d: Supplying packed meals delivered to work areas, so workers need not remove PPE or leave the line

distractorExplanations.b: Eating at workstations risks ingesting contaminants; welfare requires eating areas away from hazardous zones.
distractorExplanations.c: Rest areas beside production lines expose workers to noise and contaminants; separation from work areas is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Eating in work areas with PPE on risks contamination; facilities must allow handwashing and eating away from hazards.

options.a: Confirm the tool is safe for continuous use, since datasheet values are below the exposure limit value
options.b: Calculate exposure time against exposure limit values and plan controls under vibration regulations
options.c: Set the noise exposure zone around the tool, as vibration and noise levels are directly proportional
options.d: Replace site measurement, since manufacturer data reflect real-world use on every type of material

distractorExplanations.a: 8 m/s² is high; at that magnitude the 2.5 m/s² action value is reached in under an hour of trigger time.
distractorExplanations.c: Vibration magnitude and noise level are separate measures; noise needs its own assessment in dB(A).
distractorExplanations.d: Declared values often underestimate in-use vibration; site conditions and tool wear can raise actual exposure.

options.a: Return to full duties once a GP fit note is received, without a workplace assessment
options.b: Be redeployed to office work permanently to avoid any risk of the back injury recurring
options.c: Receive a return-to-work plan with phased duties, ergonomic review, and medical/OH advice
options.d: Be given a back support belt and retraining in lifting technique before resuming full duties

distractorExplanations.a: A fit note does not assess the job; a return-to-work plan and ergonomic review are needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Permanent redeployment without assessment is premature; a phased return with adjustments is good practice.
distractorExplanations.d: PPE and retraining do not replace a phased plan and review of the tasks that caused the injury.

options.a: Higher line speed with longer rest breaks, so the total output stays the same across each shift
options.b: Training on posture and wrist exercises at the start of each shift, with the line layout and speed unchanged
options.c: Wrist supports and anti-fatigue mats issued to each packer, as PPE is the most reliable control
options.d: Workstation height adjustment, job rotation with redesigned low-force tasks, and training on posture

distractorExplanations.a: A faster pace raises repetition and force; longer breaks later do not offset the increased ergonomic load.
distractorExplanations.b: Training and exercises are administrative; without workstation redesign the MSD risk factors remain.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE is the least reliable level of the hierarchy; engineering and task redesign should come first.

options.a: Engineering noise reduction at source combined with managed hearing protection programme
options.b: Hearing protection for affected workers as the primary control, reviewed at annual audiometry
options.c: Moving workers with tinnitus to quieter areas while other operators continue as before
options.d: Shorter shifts in noisy areas, with exposure measured once at installation of new machinery

distractorExplanations.b: Hearing protection is the last resort; long-term control should reduce noise at source first.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving affected workers helps individuals but leaves the noise hazard in place for everyone else.
distractorExplanations.d: Shorter exposure and one-off measurement are weak; noise must be reduced at source and monitored over time.

options.a: A mandatory group debriefing within 24 hours where each witness describes the event in detail
options.b: Practical support, signposting to professional help, and avoiding forced disclosure or blame
options.c: Formal witness interviews by the investigation team first, with support offered once statements end
options.d: Clinical diagnosis by a supervisor trained in first aid, followed by referral for treatment

distractorExplanations.a: Forced psychological debriefing can increase distress; PFA avoids pressuring people to recount trauma.
distractorExplanations.c: Investigation needs can wait; immediate practical and emotional support comes first in PFA.
distractorExplanations.d: PFA is not clinical diagnosis; it is practical support and signposting, not assessment by untrained staff.

options.a: A cervical support collar for each worker plus neck stretches at the start of every shift
options.b: Standing-only workstations to stop neck flexion, with no adjustment of the work height required
options.c: Adjustable bench and chair, task variation, micro-breaks, and tool balancers to reduce reach
options.d: Magnifying lamps so workers can see parts without leaning, keeping bench height as it is

distractorExplanations.a: Collars and stretches do not fix static flexion; the bench height and task layout cause the posture.
distractorExplanations.b: Standing does not correct a low work surface; static neck flexion needs height adjustment and task variation.
distractorExplanations.d: Lamps may help vision but leave the bench height unchanged, so the static neck flexion continues.

options.a: Rest areas located too far from the work zone for short breaks
options.b: Lack of a dedicated changing room for visitors to the site office
options.c: Drinking water supplied in bottles rather than from a mains tap
options.d: Inadequate washing facilities after contact with cement-based products

distractorExplanations.a: Distant rest areas are a welfare inconvenience; no washing after cement contact causes dermatitis and burns.
distractorExplanations.b: Visitor changing rooms have little health impact; skin contamination from cement is a direct physical risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Bottled water is an acceptable potable supply; inadequate washing after cement contact directly harms skin.

options.a: Existing injury, pregnancy, training, and strength relative to the task demands
options.b: Age and gender alone, using fixed weight limits for male and female workers
options.c: Job title and grade, since experienced staff are assumed to lift safely
options.d: Body weight and height, which on their own determine safe lifting capacity

distractorExplanations.b: Fixed gender limits are guidance filters; capability depends on health, training and individual strength.
distractorExplanations.c: Seniority does not ensure capability; injury, pregnancy and fitness must be considered individually.
distractorExplanations.d: Physical size alone does not determine capacity; existing injuries, pregnancy and training matter more.

options.a: Replace all seating with standing desks so staff stand for the full working day
options.b: Encourage standing breaks, walking meetings where practical, and adjustable sit-stand desks
options.c: Provide gym membership and wearable step trackers, leaving desk work patterns unchanged
options.d: Run an annual wellbeing campaign on the health risks of sitting, with posters at desks

distractorExplanations.a: Prolonged standing causes its own MSD and circulatory risks; the goal is variation between sitting and standing.
distractorExplanations.c: Out-of-work exercise does not break up sedentary work time; job design should build in movement.
distractorExplanations.d: Awareness campaigns rarely change behaviour on their own; work design changes like sit-stand desks are needed.

options.a: Anti-vibration gloves as the primary control, with tool selection reviewed only after symptoms are reported
options.b: Health surveillance as the first control, with tools replaced once screening shows early HAVS signs in workers
options.c: Selecting lower-vibration tools, maintaining equipment, limiting trigger time, and anti-vibration gloves only as supplementary
options.d: Job rotation so each operator stays just under the exposure action value, with existing high-vibration tools retained

distractorExplanations.a: Anti-vibration gloves give little protection at low frequencies; they are supplementary, not the primary control.
distractorExplanations.b: Surveillance detects harm after it starts; it checks controls are working and is not a substitute for reducing exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: Rotation without reducing tool vibration spreads exposure; lower-vibration tools and maintenance come first.

options.a: Dilute the disinfectant beyond the label instructions so vapour concentration is reduced
options.b: Issue dust masks to cleaners and keep the current product and ventilation as they are
options.c: Move the worker to another task and let a colleague continue with the same product
options.d: Review SDS, ventilation, product substitution, and health surveillance if exposure warrants

distractorExplanations.a: Over-dilution may leave surfaces inadequately disinfected; substitution and ventilation are the proper route.
distractorExplanations.b: Dust masks do not protect against vapours, and PPE is the last resort after substitution and ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving the affected worker exposes another person to the same hazard; the exposure itself must be controlled.

options.a: Set a fixed 24°C year-round, as one temperature suits every worker in an office
options.b: Manage HVAC setpoints, airflow, humidity, and allow local layering within dress code
options.c: Raise airflow from ceiling vents to the maximum to prevent stuffiness on warm days
options.d: Measure air temperature once each summer and adjust it only if it exceeds 30°C indoors

distractorExplanations.a: Thermal comfort varies by person, activity and clothing; a single fixed setpoint ignores those factors.
distractorExplanations.c: High air speeds cause draughts and discomfort; airflow should be balanced, not maximised.
distractorExplanations.d: Thermal comfort depends on humidity, air movement and activity, not one annual air temperature check.

options.a: Vehicle engine noise levels and cab hearing protection used by the driver
options.b: Hand-arm vibration from the steering wheel as the main source of back pain
options.c: Seat suspension, road conditions, driving hours, maintenance, and posture
options.d: The driver's lifting technique when loading, with seat and route not relevant

distractorExplanations.a: Noise is a separate hazard; WBV assessment focuses on seat, terrain, speed and exposure duration.
distractorExplanations.b: Steering wheel vibration is a hand-arm issue; back pain in drivers is linked to whole-body vibration via the seat.
distractorExplanations.d: Loading may add risk, but a WBV assessment must cover seat, route, driving hours and posture.

options.a: Bullying is an HR conduct matter, so it falls outside occupational health and safety duties
options.b: Bullying affects mental health only when a single incident is severe enough to be reportable
options.c: Mental health effects of bullying are personal matters, so employers wait for a medical diagnosis
options.d: Sustained bullying is a psychosocial hazard that can cause anxiety, depression, and absence

distractorExplanations.a: Bullying is recognised as a psychosocial hazard (ISO 45003); OH&S duties apply alongside HR policies.
distractorExplanations.b: Harm usually builds from sustained repeated behaviour, not from a single reportable incident.
distractorExplanations.c: Employers should assess and act on psychosocial hazards proactively, not wait for a diagnosis.

options.a: It relies on administrative control without addressing poor storage height and task design
options.b: The sign should be replaced with mandatory back belts, as PPE is more effective than signage
options.c: The wording is too generic and should instead state the maximum weight limit for each pallet
options.d: Signs are effective only when supported by annual refresher training on lifting technique

distractorExplanations.b: Swapping a sign for PPE stays at the bottom of the hierarchy; storage height and task design need changing.
distractorExplanations.c: Better wording is still an administrative control; floor-level picking remains the real problem.
distractorExplanations.d: Training plus signs are both administrative; engineering out floor-level picking is the priority.

options.a: Periodic audiometry once workers report hearing difficulty, with no baseline test at start
options.b: Baseline and periodic audiometry with record keeping and follow-up on standard threshold shifts
options.c: Noise dosimetry of each worker's shift, recorded annually to confirm protection is effective
options.d: Annual questionnaire on hearing symptoms in place of audiometry, reviewed by each worker's line manager

distractorExplanations.a: Without a baseline, threshold shifts cannot be detected; surveillance starts before or at first exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: Dosimetry measures exposure, not hearing; health surveillance means audiometric testing of the worker.
distractorExplanations.d: Questionnaires miss early loss; audiometry with occupational health review is needed, not line manager review.

options.a: Splitting each load into smaller parcels so workers lift lighter weights more often
options.b: Training workers in safe lifting technique so handling is carried out more safely
options.c: Installing conveyors, chutes, or mechanical lifts to move materials without human lifting
options.d: Providing trolleys that workers load by hand from floor level before pushing

distractorExplanations.a: Smaller loads reduce the risk but still involve manual handling; the operation is not avoided.
distractorExplanations.b: Training reduces the risk of the remaining task but does not avoid the manual handling operation.
distractorExplanations.d: Trolleys reduce carrying, but loading by hand from floor level is still manual handling.

options.a: Rotating backward weekly between days and nights so no worker stays on nights in the long term
options.b: Scheduling the heaviest and most safety-critical tasks between 3 am and 5 am when the site is quiet
options.c: Offering a night shift allowance and annual health questionnaire, with overtime unlimited on request
options.d: Fatigue risk assessment, controlled overtime, suitable lighting, and access to welfare facilities on shift

distractorExplanations.a: Backward rotation disrupts circadian rhythm most; forward rotation and fatigue management are preferred.
distractorExplanations.b: The circadian low around 3-5 am is when errors peak; critical tasks should avoid that window.
distractorExplanations.c: Pay and questionnaires do not manage fatigue, and unlimited overtime increases it.

options.a: Eyepiece height, seat support, forearm position, and break frequency from static posture
options.b: Chemical exposure from reagents and fume cupboard face velocity at the microscope bench
options.c: Lighting lux levels in the lab and screen glare from the microscope camera monitor alone
options.d: The user's eyesight prescription and the microscope's magnification settings for each task

distractorExplanations.b: Chemical exposure is a separate assessment; the ergonomic one targets posture, eyepiece height and breaks.
distractorExplanations.c: Lighting matters, but microscope ergonomics centre on eyepiece height, support and static posture.
distractorExplanations.d: Optical settings affect clarity, not the neck and back loading from static microscope posture.

options.a: Longer continuous shifts in the cold store so workers acclimatise and tolerate the cold faster
options.b: Work-rest cycles, buddy systems, warm-up breaks, and manual handling in cold conditions
options.c: Thinner gloves to improve grip on cold metal, with exposure times kept as currently planned
options.d: Heating the cold store above the product's storage temperature during each loading period

distractorExplanations.a: Acclimatisation to cold is limited; long continuous exposure increases cold injury and dexterity loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Thinner gloves increase cold injury risk; managing exposure time and warm-up breaks is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising store temperature compromises product safety; exposure must be managed through work design.

options.a: Workers spending longer in welfare units, which reduces supervision time on production tasks
options.b: Poorly maintained welfare signage, which delays workers in finding toilets during their breaks
options.c: Fatigue and dehydration from inadequate rest, hydration, and sanitary facilities reducing concentration
options.d: Higher legal penalties for welfare breaches, which divert safety budgets from accident prevention

distractorExplanations.a: Time in welfare units is not what drives accidents; poor welfare causes fatigue and reduced attention.
distractorExplanations.b: Signage is minor; inadequate rest, water and sanitation directly impair alertness and performance.
distractorExplanations.d: Penalties are a consequence, not a mechanism; the physiological effects of poor welfare raise accident risk.

options.a: Send the survey results to HR to address individual performance with low scorers
options.b: Repeat the survey in six months to confirm the trend before taking any action
options.c: Run resilience training for all staff so they can cope with conflict more effectively
options.d: Develop action plans with worker input to clarify roles and address conflict sources

distractorExplanations.a: Surveys are confidential and organisational; targeting individuals breaches trust and overlooks the work-related causes.
distractorExplanations.b: The findings already show hazards; waiting delays action on known psychosocial risks.
distractorExplanations.c: Resilience training targets the individual; role clarity and conflict need organisational fixes.

options.a: Appropriate SNR/attenuation for the noise level with correct fit and compatibility with other PPE
options.b: The highest SNR available, since more attenuation is better for every noise level and task
options.c: Comfort and low cost, so that workers accept disposable plugs for daily use without any individual fit checks
options.d: The SNR printed on the packaging, which equals the real protection achieved in the workplace

distractorExplanations.b: Over-protection causes isolation and removal of protectors; aim for a suitable level at the ear, not maximum SNR.
distractorExplanations.c: Comfort matters, but attenuation and correct fit determine protection; fit checks are needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Real-world attenuation is usually lower than the labelled SNR; fit and use must be considered.

options.a: Be archived, with a new assessment written only for the palletiser as the main remaining hazard
options.b: Be updated to cover remaining manual tasks, training on exceptions, and maintenance of new equipment
options.c: Stay unchanged until a manual handling injury shows that the awkward items need review
options.d: Cover the palletiser guarding and electrical safety, as manual handling is now minimal

distractorExplanations.a: Manual handling of awkward items still exists; the assessment must cover them as well as the new machine.
distractorExplanations.c: A significant change in work triggers review; waiting for an injury is purely reactive.
distractorExplanations.d: Minimal is not zero; awkward items still need a manual handling assessment alongside machine risks.

options.a: Barrier creams applied before wet work as the main control, with existing agents retained
options.b: Latex gloves worn for every task throughout the shift, with skin checks only when rashes appear
options.c: Substitution of harsh agents, gloves where suitable, skin care programme, and drying facilities
options.d: Cleaning hands with solvent wipes after wet work to remove residues before breaks

distractorExplanations.a: Barrier creams give unreliable protection; substitution and reducing wet contact come first.
distractorExplanations.b: Prolonged glove use causes occlusion and latex allergy; gloves need suitable selection and limited wear time.
distractorExplanations.d: Solvents strip skin oils and cause dermatitis; mild cleansers, washing and drying facilities are needed.

options.a: Place both monitors side by side with the join centred ahead, even if one screen is used most
options.b: Raise both screens above eye level so the neck extends rather than rotates during use
options.c: Increase font size on the secondary monitor so it can be read from a wider angle
options.d: Position primary screen directly ahead and angle secondary monitor to minimise sustained neck twist

distractorExplanations.a: Centring the join suits equal use; if one screen is primary, that one belongs directly ahead.
distractorExplanations.b: Screens above eye level cause neck extension strain; the top of the screen should be at or just below eye level.
distractorExplanations.c: Font size does not reduce sustained neck rotation; screen positioning is the fix.

options.a: Combining partial exposures using trigger time and manufacturer vibration data against limit values
options.b: Using the higher-vibration tool's magnitude for the full shift duration, ignoring trigger time
options.c: Adding the two tools' vibration magnitudes together and comparing the sum with the limit value
options.d: Averaging the two magnitudes and applying the result to the total trigger time in the shift

distractorExplanations.b: Exposure uses actual trigger time, not shift length; partial exposures are combined, not replaced by the maximum.
distractorExplanations.c: Magnitudes are not simply added; each partial A(8) is calculated and combined as a root sum of squares.
