distractorExplanations.d: Simple averaging misrepresents exposure; partial exposures are calculated separately and then combined.

options.a: Management signature on each ergonomic assessment is a legal precondition for its validity
options.b: Resource allocation and culture determine whether assessment findings become sustained controls
options.c: Senior managers are best placed to carry out the workstation assessments themselves
options.d: Ergonomic issues are reportable to regulators only after a manager has reviewed them

distractorExplanations.a: Signatures do not validate assessments; management support matters because it provides resources and culture.
distractorExplanations.c: Assessments need trained assessors and worker input; management's role is resourcing and leadership.
distractorExplanations.d: Reporting duties do not depend on manager review; the value of support is resources and sustained action.

options.a: Establishing the OH&S policy, ensuring resources are available, and promoting continual improvement
options.b: Delegating OH&S accountability to the safety manager, who reports results to the board annually
options.c: Setting up the hazard identification process and performing risk assessments for each department
options.d: Conducting internal audits of the OH&S management system and reporting findings to certification bodies

distractorExplanations.b: Clause 5.1 keeps accountability with top management; it can delegate tasks but not accountability for the OH&S system.
distractorExplanations.c: Hazard identification sits in clause 6.1.2 (planning); leadership under 5.1 covers policy, resources and accountability.
distractorExplanations.d: Internal audit is clause 9.2 (performance evaluation), not the leadership and commitment clause.

options.a: Plan: set objectives and processes; Do: implement; Check: monitor and measure; Act: review and improve
options.b: Plan: implement controls; Do: monitor and measure; Check: review and improve; Act: set objectives
options.c: Plan: audit the system; Do: set objectives; Check: implement controls; Act: monitor results
options.d: Plan: set objectives; Do: monitor and measure; Check: implement; Act: review and improve

distractorExplanations.b: Shifts each stage one step; Plan sets objectives, Do implements, Check monitors, and Act reviews and improves.
distractorExplanations.c: Scrambles the cycle; auditing belongs in Check and setting objectives belongs in Plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps Do and Check; implementation is the Do stage and monitoring and measuring is the Check stage.

options.a: Trends in incidents, audit findings, legal compliance status, worker feedback, and achievement of objectives
options.b: Lost-time injury rate for the year as the main input, since it gives the clearest overall picture of performance
options.c: Detailed task risk assessments from each department, reviewed line by line for scoring accuracy
options.d: Budget spend on PPE and training against forecast, as financial data show the level of commitment

distractorExplanations.b: A single lagging indicator is insufficient; management review needs audit, compliance and leading data too.
distractorExplanations.c: Management review looks at system-level performance, not line-by-line checks of individual assessments.
distractorExplanations.d: Spending shows inputs, not performance outcomes; review needs incident, audit and objective data.

options.a: Leaders model safe behavior, workers feel able to report concerns without fear, and hazards are acted on promptly
options.b: Safety rules are enforced strictly with disciplinary action for each breach, so that workers comply out of caution
options.c: Injury rates are low and the site has gone a year without a lost-time incident, shown on a gate board
options.d: The safety department owns all risk control decisions, so line managers can focus on production

distractorExplanations.b: Punitive enforcement drives under-reporting; a positive culture relies on trust and just treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: Low lagging figures can mask poor culture and under-reporting; behaviours and trust are better signs.
distractorExplanations.d: Culture is weak when safety is siloed; line managers must own safety within their own operations.

options.a: Fatigue reducing attention, reaction time, and decision quality
options.b: Boredom from low workload, which is the main cause of night errors
options.c: Peer pressure from smaller night crews to finish tasks before handover
options.d: Poor lighting levels that reduce visual acuity on night-time tasks

distractorExplanations.b: Low arousal plays a part, but fatigue from circadian disruption and long hours is the dominant factor.
distractorExplanations.c: Time pressure exists on any shift; the factor specifically linked to nights and long hours is fatigue.
distractorExplanations.d: Lighting is an environmental factor that can be engineered; the human factor tied to night work is fatigue.

options.a: Review hazards, update risk assessments, train operators, and modify safe systems of work before start-up
options.b: Start production with close supervision and review incidents after the first full month to adjust the controls
options.c: Rely on the supplier's CE declaration and manual, which cover the risks of the new machinery in use
options.d: Train maintenance staff on the new machine first, with operators trained on the job by supervisors

distractorExplanations.b: Change management requires assessment before start-up; learning from incidents afterwards is reactive.
distractorExplanations.c: Supplier documents do not address site-specific integration, layout and operator interface risks.
distractorExplanations.d: Operators face the machine daily; they need formal training before start-up, not informal on-the-job learning.

options.a: High-risk activities such as hot work, confined space entry, or electrical isolation
options.b: Routine production tasks covered by a written safe system of work and trained operators
options.c: Any task carried out by contractors on site, irrespective of its hazard level
options.d: Low-risk maintenance such as replacing light bulbs in office areas from floor level

distractorExplanations.b: Routine tasks with an adequate SSOW do not need permits; PTW is for non-routine high-risk work.
distractorExplanations.c: Contractor status alone does not trigger a permit; the hazard level of the work does.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-risk tasks are managed by normal procedures; permits are for hazardous non-routine work.

nebosh-readiness-check-hsm-systems-cultu.explanation: Permit-to-work formalizes authorization, precautions, and communication for non-routine, high-risk tasks where standard controls alone are insufficient. Permits apply where coordinated controls are essential.

options.a: Clear sequence of tasks, identified hazards, defined roles, and specified control measures
options.b: A permit signed by a manager for each task, which replaces the need for a written method
options.c: General safety rules for the site, such as wearing PPE and following the signage in all areas
options.d: A risk assessment score for the task, with methods left to the experience of the worker

distractorExplanations.b: Permits are one type of SSOW for high-risk work; a SSOW still needs a defined sequence and controls.
distractorExplanations.c: Site rules are generic; a SSOW is task-specific with its hazards, steps and roles defined.
distractorExplanations.d: Assessment identifies risk, but a SSOW must specify how the work is done safely, not leave it to discretion.

options.a: Pre-qualify competence, define H&S requirements in contract, monitor site performance, and coordinate shared risks
options.b: Check insurance and accreditation certificates, then leave site safety to the subcontractor's own supervisors
options.c: Select the lowest tender that meets technical specification, adding safety requirements once work has started
options.d: Require the subcontractor's method statement and approve it, with no further monitoring once on site

distractorExplanations.b: Certificates show credentials, not site performance; the principal contractor must monitor and coordinate.
distractorExplanations.c: Safety requirements must be set at tender and contract stage, not after work begins.
distractorExplanations.d: Approval at the start is not enough; performance must be monitored and shared risks coordinated during work.

options.a: Identifying root causes and failed controls, not only the immediate physical cause or blame on the injured person
options.b: Establishing whether the injured worker followed procedure, since most incidents result from unsafe acts
options.c: Recording the immediate cause and first aid given, as minor injuries do not justify root cause analysis
options.d: Completing the regulatory report within the legal deadline, which is the main purpose of investigation

distractorExplanations.b: Focusing on unsafe acts misses underlying causes such as design, supervision and procedures.
distractorExplanations.c: Minor injuries can share root causes with serious ones; the depth of investigation depends on potential outcome.
distractorExplanations.d: Reporting is a legal duty, but the purpose of investigation is to prevent recurrence by finding causes.

options.a: Number of completed hazard observations or near-miss reports acted upon within a set timeframe
options.b: Lost-time injury frequency rate calculated per 100,000 hours worked over the last twelve months
options.c: Number of enforcement notices and insurance claims received by the organisation this year
options.d: Days since the last lost-time injury, displayed at the gate and reported monthly to directors

distractorExplanations.b: LTIFR measures harm that has already occurred, so it is a lagging indicator.
distractorExplanations.c: Notices and claims follow failures; they are lagging, not leading, indicators.
distractorExplanations.d: A days-since count is based on injury outcomes, which makes it a lagging indicator.

options.a: Implement corrective actions, assign responsibility, set deadlines, and verify effectiveness at follow-up audit
options.b: Record the finding in the audit report and schedule the next audit, since auditing itself is the Act stage
options.c: Review the emergency plan's objectives and resources, as this belongs to the Plan stage of the cycle
options.d: Run an extra emergency drill the next day and close the finding without further follow-up or verification

distractorExplanations.b: Auditing is the Check stage; Act means taking corrective action on what the audit found.
distractorExplanations.c: Revisiting plans may follow, but responding to an audit finding with corrective action is the Act stage.
distractorExplanations.d: One drill fixes the symptom; Act requires ownership, deadlines and verification of effectiveness.

options.a: Those doing the work often have practical knowledge of hazards and solutions that management may overlook
options.b: Consultation transfers part of the legal responsibility for health and safety from the employer to workers
options.c: Workers' agreement is needed before any control can be introduced, giving them a veto on safety decisions
options.d: Consultation satisfies the requirement for risk assessment where workers agree that the risks are low

distractorExplanations.b: Consultation does not transfer duties; the employer keeps legal responsibility for health and safety.
distractorExplanations.c: Consultation means seeking and considering views, not giving workers a veto over decisions.
distractorExplanations.d: Worker views inform assessment but cannot replace the employer's duty to assess risk.

options.a: Facilitate reasonable inspection and follow up on identified issues through agreed channels
options.b: Allow the inspection only after a reportable incident, as routine inspections disrupt production
options.c: Accompany the representative and approve which areas can be seen, excluding high-risk zones
options.d: Ask the representative to submit findings to the regulator directly, rather than to management

distractorExplanations.b: Representatives may inspect routinely with reasonable notice, not merely after incidents.
distractorExplanations.c: Excluding high-risk areas defeats the purpose; the employer facilitates rather than restricts inspection.
distractorExplanations.d: Findings go to the employer for action first; bypassing management undermines agreed consultation channels.

options.a: Objectives should be measurable, communicated, and reviewed for achievement as part of the management system
options.b: Objectives should focus on lagging targets such as zero injuries, as these are easiest for staff to understand
options.c: Objectives should be set by the safety department alone so they remain consistent across sites
options.d: Objectives should be fixed for the certification cycle so performance can be compared consistently

distractorExplanations.b: Zero-injury targets can drive under-reporting; objectives should be measurable and monitorable, including leading measures.
distractorExplanations.c: Objectives need input from relevant functions and workers; setting them centrally in isolation weakens ownership.
distractorExplanations.d: Objectives must be reviewed and updated as circumstances change, not frozen for the certification cycle.

options.a: Suitable training, experience, knowledge, and behavior to perform tasks without undue risk
options.b: Holding a recognised qualification for the role, renewed every five years by the training provider
options.c: Experience of the task over several years, which outweighs any need for formal training
options.d: Passing an induction quiz on site rules, which confirms the worker can perform tasks safely

distractorExplanations.b: A qualification shows knowledge, but competence also needs experience and the ability to apply it.
distractorExplanations.c: Experience alone can embed bad habits; competence combines training, knowledge and experience.
distractorExplanations.d: Induction gives basic information; it does not demonstrate task-specific skills and experience.

options.a: It may address at-risk behaviors but fail to fix underlying system, design, or management failures
options.b: It relies on workers observing peers, which is unlawful without consent in most jurisdictions
options.c: It focuses on leading indicators, which cannot show whether accident rates are actually falling over time
options.d: It needs a large workforce to generate enough observations, so it fails in small organisations

distractorExplanations.b: Peer observation is lawful with consultation; the main limitation is that it ignores system causes.
distractorExplanations.c: Leading measures complement lagging ones; the real weakness is overlooking system and design failures.
distractorExplanations.d: Scale affects data volume, but the main limitation is that a behaviour focus misses underlying failures.

options.a: Tailor the message to the audience, use clear instructions, confirm understanding, and provide accessible reference material
options.b: Issue the full written procedure to every worker and require a signature confirming they have read it in full
options.c: Brief supervisors in detail and rely on them to cascade the procedure informally to their teams at the start of shift
options.d: Display the procedure on posters at the chemical store, as visual communication reaches every literacy level

distractorExplanations.b: Signatures prove receipt, not understanding; communication should be tailored and comprehension checked.
distractorExplanations.c: Informal cascades distort messages; workers need clear direct instruction with understanding confirmed.
distractorExplanations.d: Posters help but do not confirm understanding or cover detail; combine methods and check comprehension.

options.a: Provide a structured forum for management and worker representatives to discuss hazards, monitoring, and improvement
options.b: Take over day-to-day safety decisions from line managers, so supervisors can focus on production targets
options.c: Investigate every serious incident in place of management, as committees are independent of the employer
options.d: Approve the annual safety budget and sign off risk assessments, which gives worker members joint legal accountability

distractorExplanations.b: Committees advise and review; line management keeps day-to-day responsibility for controls.
distractorExplanations.c: Committees may review incidents, but investigation remains a management responsibility.
distractorExplanations.d: Committees do not create joint legal accountability; the employer keeps the legal duties.

options.a: Register of applicable legislation, compliance evaluation dates, findings, and corrective actions
options.b: Signed copy of the health and safety policy displayed at reception, with the date of last revision
options.c: Training matrix showing which workers have completed induction and refresher courses this year
options.d: Certificate of ISO 45001 certification issued by the external body, which confirms legal compliance

distractorExplanations.b: A policy shows commitment, not evaluation of compliance with specific legal requirements.
distractorExplanations.c: Training records support competence but do not show compliance evaluation across legal duties.
distractorExplanations.d: Certification shows conformity with the standard; it is not a confirmation of legal compliance.

options.a: Engineering or redesign solutions that make the safe way the easy way, supported by supervision and training
options.b: Disciplinary action for each worker caught bypassing guards, with a written warning issued on the spot
options.c: Retraining all operators on guarding rules and increasing supervision at the start of every shift
options.d: Warning signs on each guard and a toolbox talk on amputation risk, repeated until the shortcuts stop

distractorExplanations.b: Discipline addresses behaviour but not why the shortcut is attractive; redesign removes the incentive.
distractorExplanations.c: Training and supervision are administrative controls; recurring shortcuts point to a design problem.
distractorExplanations.d: Signs and talks are low on the hierarchy; engineering out the shortcut is more reliable.

options.a: Workplace inspections, behavioural observations, and environmental sampling planned before incidents occur
options.b: Accident investigations, ill-health reports, and analysis of near misses after they have been reported
options.c: Insurance claim reviews, enforcement notice tracking, and sickness absence data gathered each quarter
options.d: Lost-time injury rates, first-aid treatments, and damage-only incidents compared with the previous year's figures

distractorExplanations.b: These are reactive (passive) monitoring methods based on events that have already happened.
distractorExplanations.c: Claims, notices and absence are lagging data; proactive monitoring checks conditions before harm.
distractorExplanations.d: These measure outcomes after events, making them reactive rather than proactive monitoring.

options.a: A director or the most senior person in the organization to show board-level commitment
options.b: The health and safety manager, as the person responsible for writing and maintaining it
options.c: The safety committee chair, so the policy reflects agreement between workers and management
options.d: Each line manager for their own department, to show local ownership of the arrangements

distractorExplanations.b: The safety manager may draft it, but the most senior person signs to show top-level commitment.
distractorExplanations.c: Consultation shapes the policy, but signature by the most senior person shows organisational ownership.
distractorExplanations.d: Local ownership matters, but the overall policy is signed by a director or the most senior person.

options.a: Remaining staff face higher workload, stress, and unfamiliar tasks while controls and supervision may be stretched
options.b: Redundancy consultation suspends the employer's duty to update risk assessments until restructuring ends
options.c: Fewer workers on site raises the per-person exposure limits set under occupational exposure standards
options.d: Safety representatives lose their statutory role during redundancy consultation, so inspections stop

distractorExplanations.b: Duties continue during restructuring; changes in roles trigger assessment review, not suspension.
distractorExplanations.c: Exposure limits do not change with headcount; the risk arises from workload, stress and lost expertise.
distractorExplanations.d: Representatives keep their functions during restructuring; the risk comes from workload and lost expertise.

options.a: To transfer legal liability for safety from the organisation to the named individuals in each role
options.b: To ensure all significant OH&S tasks are allocated to competent people with clear accountability
options.c: To satisfy the certification body's documentation requirement, which is the main reason roles are listed
options.d: To give the safety department authority over line managers on decisions affecting production

distractorExplanations.a: Defining roles allocates tasks; the organisation's legal duties are not transferred to individuals.
distractorExplanations.c: Documentation supports certification, but the purpose is clear allocation of tasks and accountability.
distractorExplanations.d: Line managers keep responsibility; roles clarify who does what rather than shifting authority to safety staff.

options.a: Certification auditors check legal compliance and can issue enforcement notices for breaches found
options.b: Certification auditors assess conformity to the standard for third-party certification decisions
options.c: Internal audits are optional under ISO 45001, so the certification audit is the only audit required
options.d: Internal auditors must be external consultants, while certification auditors may be company staff

distractorExplanations.a: Auditors are not regulators; they assess conformity with ISO 45001 and cannot issue enforcement notices.
distractorExplanations.c: Clause 9.2 requires internal audits; certification audits do not replace them.
distractorExplanations.d: Reversed; internal auditors can be staff if objective, while certification auditors are independent third parties.

options.a: Toolbox talks where supervisors invite workers to raise hazards and respond to them
options.b: Workers routinely bypass interlocks and managers tolerate it to meet output targets
options.c: Near misses are logged, investigated and tracked to closure with feedback to reporters
options.d: Senior leaders conduct walkabouts and visibly act on the issues that workers raise

distractorExplanations.a: Two-way toolbox talks are a positive culture indicator, not a sign of failed culture.
distractorExplanations.c: Tracking near misses with feedback to reporters shows a healthy reporting culture.
distractorExplanations.d: Visible leadership acting on findings is a sign of positive culture, not of failure.

options.a: Leading: injury frequency and severity rates; Lagging: completed racking inspections and closed actions
options.b: Leading: completed racking inspections and closed actions; Lagging: injury frequency and severity rates
options.c: Leading: training hours and toolbox talks held, with no lagging measures to keep the dashboard simple
options.d: Lagging: injury frequency, severity and claims cost, with leading measures added if injuries rise

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the categories; inspections and closed actions are leading measures, injury rates are lagging.
distractorExplanations.c: Leading-only sets ignore outcomes; a balanced set pairs leading measures with injury rates.
distractorExplanations.d: Lagging-only sets react to harm; leading measures should run alongside them from the start.

options.a: They are covered by the school's insurance, so the host's risk assessment does not apply
options.b: They may lack experience, awareness of workplace risks, and confidence to raise concerns
options.c: They are legally barred from any machinery work, so the risk lies in office tasks alone
options.d: They recover from injuries more slowly than adults, so lower exposure limits apply to them

distractorExplanations.a: The host employer's duties apply to work-experience students; insurance does not remove them.
distractorExplanations.c: Restrictions vary; young workers may do some machine tasks under supervision, so risks go beyond office work.
distractorExplanations.d: The concern is inexperience and immaturity, not slower recovery; specific limits apply to some agents only.

options.a: Hazard identification, risk rating, PPE issue, and annual inspection by the regulator
options.b: Policy, organizing, planning, implementation, evaluation, and continual improvement
options.c: Compliance auditing, enforcement, and penalties as the primary drivers of improvement
options.d: Behaviour-based safety, incentives, and lagging targets as the core system elements

distractorExplanations.a: These are activities, not the ILO-OSH system elements of policy, organising, planning, evaluation and improvement.
distractorExplanations.c: ILO-OSH emphasises a management system cycle, not enforcement-driven compliance.
distractorExplanations.d: Behaviour programmes and incentives are not the framework; ILO-OSH runs from policy through to improvement.

options.a: Analysis of last year's fire incident reports to identify any trends in blocked escape routes
options.b: Scheduled inspection of fire exits to confirm they are clear, signed, and doors functional
options.c: Investigating a blocked fire exit after it was reported by a visitor during an evacuation
options.d: Reviewing insurance claims for fire damage to see whether exit doors performed correctly

distractorExplanations.a: Reviewing past incidents is reactive (passive) monitoring, not active monitoring.
distractorExplanations.c: Investigating after a report is reactive; active monitoring checks before failures occur.
distractorExplanations.d: Claims follow losses; active monitoring proactively checks that controls are in place.

options.a: Wait for a named formal complaint before acting, since anonymous reports cannot be investigated fairly
options.b: Take reports seriously, investigate promptly, and implement interim controls to protect those affected
options.c: Refer the matter to the HR grievance process and await its outcome before considering safety controls
options.d: Hold a team meeting to discuss the allegations openly so that those involved can respond in front of peers

distractorExplanations.a: Anonymous reports can still be investigated; waiting leaves workers exposed to ongoing harm.
distractorExplanations.c: Bullying is a psychosocial hazard; interim protection is needed alongside any HR process.
distractorExplanations.d: Open discussion risks exposing complainants to retaliation; a confidential investigation is needed.

options.a: The organisation's commitment to health and safety and its overall aims, signed by the managing director
options.b: How the policy is implemented — roles, procedures, training, consultation, and emergency planning
options.c: The list of hazards identified in risk assessments together with their residual risk ratings
options.d: Audit results and accident statistics for the past year, to show progress against objectives

distractorExplanations.a: That is the statement of intent section, not the arrangements for putting the policy into practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Risk registers are separate records; the policy arrangements describe the implementation systems.
distractorExplanations.d: Performance data feed review; the arrangements section sets out how the policy is implemented.

options.a: Clear labelling of controls with standardised procedures for each task
options.b: High workload combined with frequent alarms and inadequate rest breaks
options.c: Regular simulator training with competency checks for control room staff
options.d: Structured shift handover using written logs and face-to-face briefing

distractorExplanations.a: Clear labelling and standard procedures reduce error; they are protective factors, not error drivers.
distractorExplanations.c: Simulator training and competency checks lower error likelihood rather than increase it.
distractorExplanations.d: Structured handover reduces information loss between shifts; it is a control against error.

options.a: Adopt the larger site's procedures at both sites immediately, as they reflect the dominant practice
options.b: Harmonize procedures through consultation, risk assessment review, and a controlled transition plan
options.c: Keep both sets running in parallel until an incident shows which procedure performs better
options.d: Ask the certification body to choose the procedure that best meets ISO 45001 clause wording

distractorExplanations.a: Imposing one site's rules without review may miss the other site's risks; harmonise through assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Conflicting rules create confusion; waiting for incidents to decide is reactive.
distractorExplanations.d: Certification bodies do not design procedures; the organisation harmonises them through consultation.

options.a: Carrying out the hot work personally, so the issuer can confirm precautions remain effective throughout
options.b: Verifying precautions are in place, authorizing start after checks, and defining valid duration and handover
options.c: Signing the permit at the start of each shift from the control room, relying on the receiver's checks
options.d: Extending the permit at shift change by countersigning, so work continues without a new site check

distractorExplanations.a: The issuer authorises and the performing authority does the work; separating these roles is a PTW principle.
distractorExplanations.c: The issuer must verify on site that precautions are in place, not sign remotely.
distractorExplanations.d: Handover or extension requires re-verification of conditions; countersigning alone is not enough.

options.a: Paying a fine discharges the breach, so no further corrective action is legally required after a penalty
options.b: Enforcement actions signal failures in legal duties; organizations should learn and strengthen systems proactively
options.c: Enforcement notices apply only to the named manager, so the wider organisation need not change systems
options.d: Inspectors share responsibility for workplace safety, so an inspected site is presumed compliant

distractorExplanations.a: Fines punish; the employer must still correct the failure and comply with any notice served.
distractorExplanations.c: Notices are usually served on the employer; system changes are needed to comply.
distractorExplanations.d: Inspectors do not take on employer duties; passing an inspection is not a presumption of compliance.

options.a: Replaces workplace inspections, since near-miss data show every active hazard
options.b: Can reveal recurring hazards and control failures before serious injuries occur
options.c: Gives an accurate lost-time injury rate for comparison with industry benchmarks
options.d: Proves that controls are effective when near-miss numbers fall from year to year

distractorExplanations.a: Near-miss data depend on reporting rates; inspections are still needed to find unreported hazards.
distractorExplanations.c: Near-miss trends are leading data; LTIFR comes from injury records, not near misses.
distractorExplanations.d: Falling near-miss counts may reflect under-reporting rather than better controls.

options.a: Signing the safety policy and chairing the annual review, while leaving site contact to the safety staff
options.b: Participating in site walks, asking workers about hazards, and resourcing fixes for identified issues
options.c: Announcing safety bonuses tied to zero injuries, so workers see that leaders value safety outcomes
options.d: Commissioning external audits each year and circulating the reports to managers for action

distractorExplanations.a: Signing and chairing are necessary but are not visible felt leadership, which needs presence on site.
distractorExplanations.c: Zero-injury bonuses can suppress reporting; felt leadership is about engagement and acting on issues.
distractorExplanations.d: Audits are useful, but visible felt leadership requires leaders' personal involvement on site.

options.a: Rely on the contractor's own risk assessments, as the client has no duties once work is outsourced
options.b: Coordinate induction, permit rules, chemical controls, and emergency procedures for the contractor's activities
options.c: Brief the contractor's manager once at contract start, with no induction needed for night-shift staff
options.d: Require contractors to follow day-shift procedures, as emergency cover at night mirrors the day

distractorExplanations.a: The client keeps duties for site hazards and must coordinate; outsourcing does not remove them.
distractorExplanations.c: Each worker needs induction on site hazards and emergency arrangements, including night-shift staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Night work has reduced staffing and lone-working risks; emergency arrangements must reflect that.

options.a: Review each incident report in full detail, so directors can decide disciplinary outcomes
options.b: See performance trends, significant risks, and whether the system is improving over time
options.c: Track lost-time injuries as the single headline figure, since it best reflects board priorities
options.d: Demonstrate certification status to clients, as the dashboard is mainly a marketing tool

distractorExplanations.a: Boards need strategic oversight, not case-level detail or disciplinary decisions.
distractorExplanations.c: A single lagging figure hides risk trends; dashboards should combine leading and lagging data.
distractorExplanations.d: Board dashboards support governance and decision-making, not marketing to clients.

options.a: Conducting a planned noise survey before exposure changes on the new production line
options.b: Reviewing completed accident investigation reports and sickness absence data for patterns
options.c: Performing a scheduled audit of permit-to-work records against the site procedure
options.d: Carrying out a proactive ergonomic walkthrough of workstations in the packing area

distractorExplanations.a: Planned surveys are active (proactive) monitoring, not passive monitoring.
distractorExplanations.c: Scheduled audits check systems before failure occurs, which is active monitoring.
distractorExplanations.d: Walkthroughs check conditions before harm occurs; that is active monitoring.

options.a: Assigning a safety officer to review each business decision after approval, to flag issues for correction
options.b: Considering OH&S impacts in procurement, design, scheduling, and change — not treating safety as an afterthought
options.c: Reporting safety statistics at board meetings, while operational decisions remain with production teams
options.d: Including safety in the annual business plan as a standalone section owned by the safety department

distractorExplanations.a: Post-approval review is still an afterthought; OH&S should shape decisions from the start.
distractorExplanations.c: Reporting statistics is monitoring; integration means OH&S informs procurement, design and change.
distractorExplanations.d: A standalone section keeps safety siloed; integration embeds it across every business function.

options.a: Attend the general site induction for new operatives, which covers everything a director needs to know
options.b: Receive induction on legal duties, the H&S policy, significant risks, and how performance is measured
options.c: Complete a full NEBOSH qualification before taking up the post, as directors must be safety experts
options.d: Delegate safety decisions to the H&S manager until a year's operational experience has been gained

distractorExplanations.a: Operative induction covers site rules, not directors' legal duties and governance of performance.
distractorExplanations.c: Directors need sufficient understanding of duties and risks, not a full professional qualification.
distractorExplanations.d: Directors keep accountability from day one; delegation does not remove the need for induction.

options.a: Translating the full safety policy into each language and issuing it by email to every worker
options.b: Toolbox talks with interpreters/visual aids, pictorial signage, and safety reps from diverse crews
options.c: Using bilingual supervisors to relay instructions, with no worker feedback channel in other languages
options.d: Holding a single site-wide meeting in English with a translated summary handed out afterwards

distractorExplanations.a: Written translations may not reach workers with low literacy; face-to-face and visual methods work better.
distractorExplanations.c: Consultation is two-way; relaying instructions without feedback is communication, not consultation.
distractorExplanations.d: One English meeting excludes non-English speakers from discussion; consultation needs participation.

options.a: Prove that training has transferred legal responsibility for safe working from the employer to the employee
options.b: Demonstrate competence, identify refresher needs, and provide evidence for audits and investigations
options.c: Replace the need for supervision once a worker's record shows the course has been completed
options.d: Satisfy the regulator's requirement that every course be logged within 24 hours of delivery

distractorExplanations.a: Training records do not transfer duties; the employer remains legally responsible.
distractorExplanations.c: Course completion does not remove the need for supervision, especially for new starters.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no general 24-hour logging rule; records serve competence, refresher and evidence needs.

options.a: Assign responsibility to the department that owns the walkway on the site plan and close the case on that basis
options.b: Examine the shared interface, housekeeping, lighting, and rules rather than focusing only on individual fault
options.c: Interview the workers involved to establish who was at fault, then apply the disciplinary policy
options.d: Have each department investigate separately and submit its own report to the safety committee

distractorExplanations.a: Ownership on a plan does not address interface failures; the investigation should look at shared systems.
distractorExplanations.c: Focusing on individual fault misses root causes such as layout, lighting and unclear rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Separate investigations repeat the blame split; a joint investigation of the interface is needed.

options.a: The document reaches its fixed annual review date, which is the only valid trigger for revision
options.b: There is significant organizational change, new legal duties, or findings from audit/incident review
options.c: A certification body requests it, as policy revision falls outside the organisation's own review
options.d: A new safety manager is appointed and wants the policy to reflect their personal approach

distractorExplanations.a: Periodic review is good practice, but change, new law and audit findings are also valid triggers.
distractorExplanations.c: The organisation owns its policy review; it does not depend on a certification body's request.
distractorExplanations.d: A change of personnel is not a trigger by itself unless it changes the organisation or arrangements.

options.a: Launch the app with a reward for the highest number of reports per shift, so participation rises quickly
options.b: Use report data to identify the workers who raise the most hazards and review their performance at annual appraisals
options.c: Train all shifts on use, act on reports promptly, feed trends into management review, and protect reporters from retaliation
options.d: Collect reports through the app and review them at the annual audit, so trends are analysed in one batch

distractorExplanations.a: Volume rewards encourage trivial or false reports; culture depends on acting on reports and on trust.
distractorExplanations.b: Linking reports to appraisals deters reporting; reporters must be protected, not scrutinised.
distractorExplanations.d: Annual batch review delays action; reports need a prompt response and regular trend analysis.
